items.name: Chien-Hsiang Lin
items.title: When the ocean gets too warm: lessons from ancient fish communities

abstract.authors: Chien-Hsiang Lin 林千翔
abstract.abstract: How do marine communities respond when the ocean becomes exceptionally warm, and does cooling bring them back? Modern observations capture rapid ecological change, but rarely span the full course of disruption and recovery. Fossil records offer a unique, longer view. We use tiny fish otoliths preserved in deep-sea sediments to reconstruct lanternfish communities in the tropical western Pacific across six exceptionally warm periods. We found that lanternfishes are abundant members of ocean food webs, and that their fossils allow us to track changes in fish production, diversity, community composition, and body size over hundreds of thousands of years. Our record links extreme warmth to declines in fish production and diversity, accompanied by shifts in body-size structure. We develop a biomass-flux proxy, asking whether shifts toward larger fish can conceal a decline in the fish mass represented through time. Differences between pre- and post-warming size distributions also raise the possibility of delayed or altered recovery. By comparing events with contrasting warming histories, we examine how warming intensity, duration, and rate relate to ecological disruption, and whether different aspects of community structure and biomass flux recover together during subsequent cooling. The central question is not simply whether fish communities decline under extreme warmth, but how they reorganize and whether the communities that emerge afterward resemble those that came before. These deep-time records provide a long-term perspective on the vulnerability and resilience of marine ecosystems in a warming world.

items.name: Mu-Hsiang Wang
items.title: Climatic warming drives directional changes in fish population dynamics across the Atlantic Ocean

abstract.authors: Mu-Hsiang Wang*, Ruo-Yu Pan, Yun-Wei Chou, Chih-hao Hsieh, Chun-Wei Chang
abstract.abstract: Ocean warming alters marine population dynamics, yet species differ in their sensitivity to climatic change. We used empirical dynamic modeling (EDM) to quantify causal influences of sea surface temperature (SST) on fish biomass across multiple Atlantic fisheries surveys. Overall, SST causal strength was positively associated with the magnitude of biomass trends, and this relationship strengthened with increasing regional SST trends, indicating widespread coupling between ocean warming and fish population dynamics. Mixed-effects models showed that SST causal strength decreased with species’ thermal preference but increased with habitat depth range, suggesting stronger SST–biomass coupling in colder-water species and those with broader depth ranges. Among biomass-declining populations, 40.8% exhibited significant SST–biomass causal convergence, with cold-water species predominating. Further analysis revealed that species with lower thermal preferences, lower latitudes, and western Atlantic distributions were more likely to experience both biomass declines and significant SST causal effects. Collectively, our results identify ecological and geographic characteristics associated with SST-linked fish biomass declines and provide a broad-scale framework for assessing the vulnerability of marine populations and fisheries to ocean warming.

items.name: Namfon Booncharoen
items.title: Bridging invasion ecology and climate tracking: Biotic interactions modulate early establishment success

abstract.authors: Namfon Booncharoen*, I-Ching Chen, Yi-Wen Chen, Cheng-Hao Lin, Cascade J.B. Sorte, Marta A. Jarzyna, Yi-Hsiu Chen
abstract.abstract: Biotic interactions are recognized as key modulators of heterogeneous range shifts under climate change, yet their influence remains difficult to test across broad spatial scales. Building on invasion ecology, we developed a framework to evaluate how recipient community structure is associated with early occupancy gains within climatically suitable space. We tested predictions from the biotic resistance versus biotic acceptance hypotheses and Darwin's naturalization versus preadaptation hypotheses. Using the Taiwan Breeding Bird Survey (>300 sites; 136 species), we compared Absence-to-Presence (AP) sites, where focal species showed occupancy gain between 2020 and 2021, with Absence-to-Absence (AA) sites where focal species remained undetected despite climatic suitability; sites were paired within species and restricted to locations with plausible propagule access. Across 428 AP–AA pairs spanning 62 species, AP sites showed higher recipient community diversity, supporting biotic acceptance over biotic resistance. Focal species were functionally similar to resident assemblages at AP than AA sites, supporting Darwin's preadaptation hypothesis; phylogenetic distinctiveness showed no effect. Morphology and climate-preference traits drove functional similarity; habitat and foraging traits differentiated more. By adapting invasion hypotheses to climate-related redistribution, our framework provides an empirically testable basis for incorporating recipient community context into predictions of species range dynamics under environmental change.

items.name: Gakuto Nihei
items.title: Plasticity within and across generations: diversity of larval feeding morphology in the two Papilio butterflies

abstract.authors: Gakuto Nihei*, Suzuki Noriyuki
abstract.abstract: Plastic responses of offspring phenotypes are triggered by their own environments, such as inducible defense (within-generation plasticity), and by environments experienced by prior generations, such as seasonal polyphenism (across-generation plasticity). In phytophagous insects, these contrasting types of phenotypic plasticity should reflect spatio and temporal variations of microhabitat and host-plant quality. Here, we examined phenotypic plasticity of larval feeding traits within and across generations in two sympatric swallowtail butterflies, Papilio memnon and Papilio xuthus, which use the same species of host-plant but depend on different microenvironment. First, we experimentally measured the inducible responses of larval morphology and feeding performance to leaf toughness. Second, we surveyed seasonal variation in egg size and hatchling morphology. Papilio memnon larvae exhibited within-generation plasticity in their head size and mandibles in response to leaf toughness, while P. xuthus did not show such flexibility. In contrast, P. xuthus exhibited across-generation plasticity in egg size and larval morphology correlated to seasonal variation of leaf toughness, while P. memnon did not show significant seasonal variation. Our results suggest that these different types of plasticity in feeding traits are adaptive to spatio and temporal variations in host-plant quality for each species.

items.name: Shan-Dar Tao
items.aff: National Museum of Natural Science, Taiwan
items.title: Cold tolerance in two tropical gecko species at their northern range limit in the Ryukyu Archipelago: implications for Bogert’s effect in Gehyra mutilata

abstract.authors: Shan-Dar Tao*
abstract.abstract: Cold stress limits tropical ectotherms' northward range expansion. We compared cold tolerance of two tropical gecko species at their northernmost range edge on Amamioshima Island, Japan. Gehyra mutilata colonized the island decades ago, and Hemidactylus frenatus arrived around 2000. We tested whether cold tolerance varies between the established northern population on Okinawa Island and the newer range on Amamioshima. Results showed differences between species. G. mutilata, highly human commensal, had a higher CTmin than H. frenatus. H. frenatus showed little geographic variation in CTmin, while G. mutilata showed none. These findings suggest differences in thermal physiology relate to human commensalism and thermoregulatory behavior, supporting their different invasion histories. The study also offers insights into Bogert's effect on G. mutilata.

items.name: Rita S.W. Yam
items.aff: Department of Bioenvironmental Systems Engineering, National Taiwan University
items.title: 2500 years of fossil Chironomid assemblages reflect non-recoverable ecosystem change of a high mountain lake in Taiwan under historical forest harvesting and global climatic change

abstract.authors: Rita S.W. Yam*, Chen-Yu Lee, Tsai-Wen Lin, Pei-Ling Wang, Stefanie Kaboth-Bahr, André Bahr, Ludvig Löwemark
abstract.abstract: High-mountain lakes are sensitive indicators of climate shifts and anthropogenic disturbances, yet paleolimnological records remain scarce on subtropical islands. We present a 2500-year high-resolution environmental reconstruction from Cuifeng Lake, Taiwan, using subfossil chironomid assemblages and sediment geochemistry (total nitrogen, TN; total organic carbon, TOC) to examine baseline climate, historical forestry, and exotic fish introductions. Prior to industrial interventions, gradual increases in TN and TOC reflected natural lake infilling. Between AD 65 and 386, increased chironomid density indicated a water-level transgression driven by a warm, humid climate. In the twentieth century, clear-cut logging (1915–1982) inflicted a severe hydrological shock, shifting the chironomid community and expanding filter-feeders from 22.4% to 33.4%. Post-AD 1989, introducing exotic benthivorous fishes triggered a severe multi-trophic regime shift. This biological invasion collapsed chironomid density and caused an unprecedented exponential upsurge in TN and TOC via metabolic excretion and substrate bioturbation. While chironomid communities showed ecological resilience to macro-climatic transitions, historical logging combined with modern biological invasions has locked this alpine system into a permanently altered, non-recoverable state, shifting modern conservation and restoration baselines.

items.name: Zong-Yu Shen
items.aff: The University Museum, The University of Tokyo
items.title: Divergent fates after parallel historical isolation: habitat area predicts demographic resilience in Japan’s national butterfly across replicated continent-island systems

abstract.authors: Zong-Yu Shen*, Jen-Pan Huang, Yu Okamura, Yu-Feng Hsu, Tzong-Han Lin, My-Hang Le, Shao-Ji Hu, Li-Wei Wu, Masaya Yago
abstract.abstract: Island biogeography predicts that island area governs species richness, yet whether this relationship extends to population-level resilience within species remains poorly understood. Indeed, species-level extinction typically follows a longer process of population loss, making population resilience an urgent conservation target. Testing this requires a species spanning continental and island systems. Sasakia charonda, the national butterfly of Japan and an umbrella species of the Satoyama landscape, provides such a system, with four subspecies spanning continental East Asia, Japan, and Taiwan. Using range-wide sampling and the first chromosome-level reference genome, we integrated phylogenomics, demographic inference, and genotype-environment association to delimit five conservation units (CUs). Two island CUs sharing parallel founder-effect signatures show distinct demographic trajectories, with the larger, more latitudinally extensive island (Japan) maintaining more subpopulations and greater effective population size than the smaller one (Taiwan). A similar pattern appears on the continent, where a highland-restricted lineage with few subpopulations is vulnerable. Habitat area may thus shape demographic resilience through the number of subpopulations a landscape can sustain. The most vulnerable CUs also face the highest projected climate mismatch, compounding their risk. These findings suggest island biogeography principles may extend from species richness to within-species demographic resilience, informing actionable conservation strategies.

items.name: Chi-Ying Lee
items.title: A zombie parasitism: How a parasitic barnacle takes over its hosts?

abstract.authors: Hsiang-Yin Chen, Chih-Cheng Tsai, Xin-Ci Liang, Yun Chen, Hung-Chang Liu, Chien-Hsun Lee, Jean-Yves Toullec, Wen-San Huang, Benny K.K. Chan, Chi-Ying Lee*
abstract.abstract: Rhizocephalans are highly modified and specialized parasites of other crustaceans. Adult rhizocephalan consists of an external reproductive sac (the externa), which is still connected to an internal system of rootlets that ramifies throughout the interior of the host (the interna). These parasites exert control over the host in order to complete their life cycle. We studied the mechanism of host control using an association of the shore crab Metopograpsus thukuhar parasitized by Polyascus planus. First, control over host's reproduction is sex-specific. For females, production of vitellogenin, is not affected, while ovarian maturation is arrested. As for males, production of vitellogenin is induced and testicular maturation hardly affected. Expression of androgenic gland hormone in parasitized males is significantly decreased. Second, the immunity of parasitized hosts is suppressed, with a higher number of hemolymph bacteria, a lower number of circulating hemocytes, and no significant immune responses to tissue-invading rootlets. Necrosis of circulating hemocytes is a key component of the parasite-induced immunosuppression. Finally, an ecdysteroid surge is required to drive the molt cycle, ovarian cycle and secretory cycle of the colleteric gland of sexually mature externa, which collectively influence the reproductive output of (number of larvae released from) the externa.

items.name: Ming-Chung Chiu
items.aff: Department of Entomology, National Taiwan University
items.title: Phenotypic Similarities between Parasitized Mantids and Male-Specific Wing Dimorphism: Juvenile Hormone as a Possible Shared Regulatory Mechanism

abstract.authors: Ming-Chung Chiu, Zih-Ting Chang, Chieh-Ting Tsai, Cheng-Yu Shih
abstract.abstract: Horsehair worms manipulate insect hosts to enter water, but their effects begin earlier. In Hierodula mantids, infection causes gonadal reduction and alters male wing shape and grooved basiconic antennal sensilla. Artificial infections show that these sex-dependent effects emerge during host sexual differentiation, suggesting interference with male differentiation rather than generalized developmental arrest or juvenilization. The uninfected mantid Amantis nawai provides a natural parallel. Taiwanese males are macropterous or micropterous, whereas females are exclusively micropterous. Macropterous males have more antennal sensilla than micropterous males, whose counts are intermediate between macropterous males and females. This pattern suggests partially shared, sex-dependent regulation. Juvenile hormone (JH) may link these traits. In A. nawai, wing-bud differences appear by the third instar, whereas differences in antennal sensilla appear only in adults. JH declines during the final instar, but micropterous males show a transient mid-instar increase. DZNep treatment during this window preliminarily increased wing length and sensilla number and induced wing-lifting. Although causality and DZNep specificity remain unconfirmed, these results support a two-stage model: early establishment of wing morphs followed by JH-sensitive terminal differentiation of wings and antennae. Natural variation may modify this system in A. nawai, while horsehair worms may disrupt the same developmental module in Hierodula.

items.name: Shotaro Tani
items.aff: Center for Ecological Research, Kyoto University
items.title: Natural history and comparative phylogeography of horsehair worms, parasites cycling between aquatic and terrestrial hosts

abstract.authors: Shotaro Tani*, Koichiro Kawai, Takuya Sato
abstract.abstract:
Hairworms (Nematomorpha) have a two-phase life cycle: larvae infect aquatic benthic invertebrates, which are then eaten by terrestrial insects in which the worms mature. Mature worms drive their hosts into water, a textbook case of the extended phenotype. However, fundamental information on host range and distribution remains scarce in Asia, including Japan.
Focusing on three Japanese species of the genus Chordodes, we compiled host lists from field surveys and conducted infection experiments on definitive hosts. The results indicated that host specificity is set not by the likelihood of encounter but by a physiological filter: whether larvae can establish and develop once ingested.
Furthermore, molecular phylogeographic analysis uncovered distinct patterns of geographic genetic structure for each species. Given that host dispersal drives gene flow in these parasites—which have limited mobility themselves—we had anticipated high levels of gene flow resulting from the combined dispersal capabilities of both aquatic and terrestrial hosts; however, the data actually revealed genetic divergence associated with specific mountain ranges.
In this talk I use host specificity as a lens for reading these patterns, and ask which of the two environments has shaped the distribution of these parasites.
abstract.affiliation: Center for Ecological Research, Kyoto University

items.name: Asami Kajimoto
items.title: Sex-specific reproductive strategies in the rhizocephalan

abstract.authors: Asami Kajimoto*, Kenji Toyota
abstract.abstract:
Rhizocephalans (Thecostraca: Cirripedia) are parasitic barnacles that infect diverse decapod crustaceans, including hermit crabs, crabs, and shrimps. Peltogasterella gracilis, a parasite of pagurid hermit crabs, exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism and sex-specific settlement. Female larvae settle on hermit crab hosts, whereas male larvae settle on immature females and subsequently develop into dwarf males. Here, we investigated how these sex-specific settlement patterns are associated with seasonal sex-ratio variation, sex-biased gene expression, and molecular responses during settlement.
Field surveys revealed seasonal variation in offspring sex ratio: male larvae were absent during summer but were produced from autumn to the following spring. This seasonal pattern was suggested to correspond to the availability of unparasitized hosts for female larvae and immature female parasite bodies for male larvae. Comparative transcriptomic analyses of male and female cyprids identified sex-biased genes potentially involved in sex-specific morphology and settlement. Additionally, comparison of gene expression responses to sex-specific settlement substrates revealed distinct molecular responses between male and female cyprids.
These results suggest that seasonal sex allocation and sex-specific molecular mechanisms of settlement are closely linked in P. gracilis, providing a basis for divergent reproductive strategies between male and female larvae.

items.name: Takumi Takamatsu
items.aff: Center for Ecological Research, Kyoto University
items.title: A unique mechanism of male-killing induced by symbiotic viruses

abstract.authors: Takumi TAKAMATSU*, Maki N. INOUE
abstract.abstract:
Maternally inherited female-biased sex ratios are found in many arthropods, and one cause is male-killing, in which males die selectively during embryonic or larval development, resulting in all-female broods. In insects, male-killing is mostly caused by bacteria such as Wolbachia, but some symbiotic viruses also induce it.
Homona magnanima (Lepidoptera: Tortricidae) is a major pest of tea plants in East Asia. Segmented double-stranded RNA viruses, Osugoroshi viruses 1–3 (OGV1–3; Partitiviridae), have been identified as the causative agents of male-killing in this species. Unlike bacterial male-killing, which typically occurs during embryogenesis, OGV-induced male death occurs at the larval stage: OGVs are transovarially transmitted and, in young male larvae, cause molting failure and degeneration of the midgut epithelium. Although 27 dsRNA segments—three encoding RNA-dependent RNA polymerases and 24 encoding proteins of unknown function—have been detected in infected hosts, the mechanism by which OGVs kill males remains unknown.
Here, we report the results of omics analyses and analyses of the endocrine system in OGV-infected male larvae, which suggest an endocrine disruption distinct from that involved in bacterial male-killing.

items.name: Takanori Nishino
items.title: Entomopathogen-related fungal symbionts on female hindleg of dinidorid stinkbugs

abstract.authors: Takanori Nishino*, Minoru Moriyama, Hiromi Mukai, Masahiko Tanahashi, Takema Fukatsu
abstract.abstract:
Female dinidorid stinkbugs (Hemiptera: Heteroptera: Dinidoridae) possess a distinctive organ on the hind tibiae that has been long interpreted as a ear. In Megymenum gracilicorne, we found that this organ is, in fact, an external symbiotic organ.
This organ have numerous pores connected to secretory cells, from which fungal hyphae reside. During oviposition, the female applies these fungi onto the eggs with "egg-smearing". Subsequently, the hyphae cover the egg mass, providing a physical barrier to protect the parasitoid wasps.
Each female harbor several fungal species, and community composition differed among individuals, localities, and years. This observation suggests the hypothesis that females reacquire fugal symbionts from the environment with each generation. 
The fungi are predominantly members of the family Cordycipitaceae, a group consisting of rich entomopathogens, whereas the symbiotic fungi exhibit mild pathogenicity. Consequently, it is plausible that females selectively cultivate less pathogenic fungi within the entomopathogen-relateds. 
The mechanisms through which female insects select fungi, and tolerate or avoid infection, remain unclear. However, our findings indicate that other Diniidridae insects also possess analogous organs and exhibit the egg-smearing, whereas Cordycipitaceae dominance appears restricted to Megymenum.  Here, we would like to discuss the potential evolutionary history based on what is currently known.

items.name: Hsuan-Wien Chen
items.title: A slightly more complicated model for pattern of parasitism in nature

abstract.authors: Hsuan-Wien Chen* and Wei-Chung Liu
abstract.abstract: In our earlier work, we developed a simple model to describe patterns of parasitism in nature. In this original model, parasite species were randomly seeded within a food web and subsequently transmitted among host species through predator–prey trophic interactions. At the macroscopic level, the model successfully reproduced the observed pattern of parasite diversity across host species. However, at the microscopic level, it was less successful in reproducing the observed parasite diversity of individual host species. In a more recent model, we incorporated additional mechanisms, including competition among parasite species, but these modifications resulted in only limited improvement in explaining patterns of parasitism at the microscopic level. In the present study, we therefore return to the framework of our original model and introduce a slightly more complex transmission mechanism that more realistically represents the biology of parasite complex life cycles. We examine whether incorporating this additional biological realism improves the model's ability to reproduce observed patterns of parasite diversity at both the macroscopic and microscopic levels.

items.name: Wan-Hsuan Cheng
items.title: The expansion of community level niche breadth in response to long term nutrient stress enhances ecosystem multifunctionality

abstract.authors: Wan-Hsuan Cheng*, Masayuki Ushio, Chao-Chen Lai, Fuh Kwo Shiah, Chun-Wei Chang, Chih-hao Hsieh, Takeshi Miki
abstract.abstract: Environmental change can alter ecosystem multifunctionality (EMF) by reshaping biological communities, yet ecological frameworks often assume that community–environment and community–function relationships remain constant over time. This assumption overlooks the possibility that shifting selective pressures can modify species' niches and progressively alter these ecological relationships. Here, we investigated how long-term resource stress influences community niche dynamics and their consequences for EMF using a 9-year biweekly time series from a subtropical reservoir. We measured microbial community utilization profiles of 31 carbon substrates, quantifying community niche breadth (NB) as the number of substrates utilized and EMF as the summed utilization rates across all substrates, within moving annual windows. Because carbon utilization was co-limited by phosphorus, resource stress (re-oligotrophication) was quantified via phosphate scarcity, variability, and depletion. Prolonged nutrient stress drove progressive expansion of community-level NB and strengthened its positive relationship with EMF, such that broader NB contributed increasingly to EMF under resource limitation. Consequently, both NB expansion and its enhanced functional contribution jointly elevated EMF over time. Parallel population-level analyses confirmed our predictions at the population level, though with weaker effects, and revealed that community NB broadening arose from two concurrent mechanisms: species turnover and within-population niche plasticity. Our findings demonstrate that environmental change reshapes niches and their functional consequences through multi-level pathways, challenging static assumptions and underscoring the need for dynamic frameworks to predict ecosystem functioning.

items.name: Huiyu Wang
items.title: Fish migratory strategies drive contrasting life-history and demographic responses to environmental gradients

abstract.authors: Hui-Yu Wang*, Genki Sahashi, Kenta Anraku, Akihiko Goto, Wei-Ren Lin, Mark Yen-Ting Liu, Sheng-Feng Shen, and Kentaro Morita
abstract.abstract: Understanding how organisms respond to environmental heterogeneity is essential for predicting population persistence under climate change. In salmonids, anadromous and landlocked forms represent alternative life-history strategies, yet how these strategies interact with environmental variation to shape demographic responses remains unclear. We quantified temperature- and density-dependent life-history and demographic variation across a ~21° latitudinal gradient (24–45°N) in masu salmon (Oncorhynchus masou). Environmental heterogeneity generated two major life-history trade-offs: a latitudinal shift in lifetime reproductive allocation between semelparity and iteroparity, and a temperature- and density-dependent trade-off between maturation and survival. These trade-offs produced contrasting demographic responses between migratory forms. Anadromous populations, distributed in colder, high-latitude environments, exhibited stronger environmental regulation, higher net reproductive rates (R₀) under cool conditions, but steeper declines in R₀ with warming. In contrast, landlocked populations showed weaker environmental regulation and relatively stable R₀ across temperature gradients. Our results demonstrate that environmentally mediated energy-allocation trade-offs determine the sensitivity of population growth to warming and highlight the importance of intraspecific life-history diversity for predicting demographic responses to environmental change.

items.name: Sing-Pei Yu
items.title: Long-term variation in trait allometry across a population bottleneck and ecosystem change in a freshwater goby

abstract.authors: Sing-Pei Yu¹*, Yun-Ching Chang², Yoichiro Sakai³, Chao-Li Huang², Takefumi Nakazawa¹, Cheng-Han Tsai¹
abstract.abstract: Morphological traits scale with body size and vary over time, providing a unique way to track trait variation within animal populations beyond changes in average size. Here we examine whether relationships between body features and body size of an endemic goby change across the population decline and environmental change. We measure 11 morphological features with size in 3,856 individual specimens of the Gymnogobius isaza, collected in 22 years in Lake Biwa. We find that size-dependency in morphological features varied among years, associated with changes in eutrophic conditions, food availability, and fishery and invasion history for potential competitors and predators. After the goby stock decline, pelvic-fin and left pectoral-fin lengths increase less sharply with body size, whereas eye diameter increases more sharply. Moreover, the association between environmental conditions and allometric relationships differed before and after the population decline. Allometric growth across functional traits clearly reorganizes after a severe demographic bottleneck, suggesting plastic allometric responses may themselves evolve adaptively under ecosystem transitions.

items.name: Pei-Chi Ho
items.aff: Institute of Oceanography, National Taiwan University
items.title: Effect of nutrient supply and prey composition on plankton stoichiometry and trophic structure in marine food webs

abstract.authors: Pei-Chi Ho*, Chia-Ting Chen, Wei-Ting Chen, Tamaha Yamaguchi, Sachiko Horii, Jun Nishioka, Ichiro Yasuda, Hiroaki Saito
abstract.abstract: Plankton stoichiometry (C:N:P ratios in biomass) critically influences the trophic transfer efficiency and secondary production in marine food webs. Nutrient supply and light intensity are key factors affecting phytoplankton stoichiometry. In addition to resource supply, the trophic strategy body of plankton is associated with the values and variability of their stoichiometry: plankton trophic strategy shift from autotrophy to heterotrophy with body size, and stoichiometric variability is lower in heterotrophic zooplankton. In this study, we collected size-fractioned particulate organic matter (POM) and zooplankton and measured the carbon (C), nitrogen (N), and phosphorus (P) contents in different size fractions along the Kuroshio-affected region in the eastern Japan. We investigated (1) the relationship between nitrogenous : phosphorus nutrient concentrations and size-fractioned POM C:N:P ratios, which reflect the stoichiometry of unicellular protists, (2) the relationship between heterotrophy : autotrophic protist ratio and POM C:N:P ratios, (3) the relationship between body size and C:N:P ratios of size-fractioned plankton. Our study reveals that body size is strongly related to the stoichiometry of plankton. Plankton C:N and C:P ratio decreased with body size and heterotrophy, and variation of C:N ratio across sampling sites are smaller in large-size zooplankton. Plankton N:P ratio exhibited a unimodal pattern with body size, possibly reflecting the difference of growth rate of different-sized plankton.

items.name: Wei-Ting Chen
items.aff: Department of Bioenvironmental Systems Engineering, National Taiwan University
items.title: Light regime and the growth–grazing balance of pico- and nanoplankton over the Taiwan Bank

abstract.authors: Wei-Ting Chen*, Shi-Rong Su, Yen-Po Wang, Feng‐Hsun Chang
abstract.abstract: Semidiurnal internal tides generated in the Luzon Strait shoal and break on the slope south of the Taiwan Bank, steepening into bores that drive cold-water run-up and generate a turbulent bottom-mixed layer (BML). Successive bores advect this cold, saline, nutrient-rich layer upslope; over the bank it outcrops, depending on the strength of turbulence and the tidal phase, sustaining the recurrent chlorophyll-rich surface water. The physical supply mechanism is well described, but the biological balance is not. Pico- and nanoplankton growth and microzooplankton grazing mortality were measured in the source region south of the tidal mixing front, in the surface layer and in the aphotic zone. Preliminary profiling placed the 1% light depth at 45 m, so the surface samples lie within the euphotic zone and the 60 m bottom-mixed layer below it. We aim to determine whether growth exceeds grazing in the surface layer, to quantify the rate at which pico- and nanophytoplankton abundance declines in the aphotic BML, and to establish the share of that loss attributable to grazing — the terms that determine whether cells transported upslope can seed the surface bloom.

items.name: Yu-An Chen
items.aff: Atmosphere and Ocean Research Institute, The University of Tokyo
items.title: Modeling Lipid-Driven Population Dynamics of Copepod Neocalanus plumchrus in the Subarctic Pacific

abstract.authors: Yu-An Chen* and Hiroaki Saito
abstract.abstract: In high-latitude regions, studies have highlighted the significance of carbon export through ontogenetic vertical migration by copepods. This process involves accumulating lipids in the surface layer and consuming them during dormancy in the mesopelagic layer. In the subarctic Pacific, lipid storing copepods dominate the zooplankton community, making lipid pump a potentially critical component of carbon sequestration. However, it is difficult to quantify carbon flux through existing observations due to deficiency of data relating their dormancy. To address this gap, we develop a population dynamics model to simulate the life cycle of the dominant copepod Neocalanus plumchrus, incorporating storing lipid dynamics. This model includes eight developmental phases and tracks abundance, structural and lipid weight for each phase, driven by two environmental variables: temperature from the World Ocean Atlas and chlorophyll a concentration from NASA’s Aqua satellite. As the result, the model can reproduce long-term simulations of copepod population dynamics at three stations (Station A7, K2 and Papa). Moreover, it demonstrates regional differences in copepod abundance and carbon export during dormancy. This research could contribute to quantifying the amount of carbon sequestered by copepod species carrying out ontogenetic vertical migration in the subarctic Pacific.
abstract.affiliation: Atmosphere and Ocean Research Institute, The University of Tokyo

items.name: Guan-Yan Chen
items.title: Influence of Habitat Morphology on Coral Recruit Distribution

abstract.authors: Guan-Yan Chen*,
abstract.abstract: Key habitat structures can influence species coexistence, predator avoidance, resource acquisition, and reproductive success. However, previous studies of coral recruitment have largely focused on artificial structures or the effects of natural reef morphology at relatively large spatial scales. In two 8 × 8 m plots in Kāneʻohe Bay, Hawaiʻi, we used Structure-from-Motion photogrammetry to generate high-resolution orthomosaics and digital elevation models, identifying 807 coral recruits and natural reef crevices to examine habitat preferences among coral growth forms. Digitate and corymbose corals occurred more frequently within or near crevices, whereas encrusting and branching corals showed no clear preference. Crevice width was the most important morphological predictor of recruit distribution, followed by maximum depth and circularity, with preferences differing among coral growth forms. By reverse-engineering natural reefs, this study identifies key microhabitat features that promote coral recruitment, providing a pathway for restoration structure design to move beyond iterative trial-and-error toward nature-informed functional design. Our findings also suggest a potential mechanism by which structural complexity may enhance reef recovery: reefs with more abundant and diverse crevices may provide greater availability of suitable settlement habitat and refugia for coral recruits.

items.name: Yu Ting Lin
items.aff: Sesoko Marine Research Station, Tropical Biosphere Research Center, University of the Ryukyus
items.title: Taxon- and size-specific variation in coral growth between tropical and subtropical-temperate reefs of the western Pacific

abstract.authors: Yuting Vicky Lin*, Munasik Munasik, Kakaskasen Andreas Roeroe, Seiji Arakaki, Takuma Mezaki, Takashi Kawai, Jean J.B. Tanangonan, Diah Permata Wijayanti, Yoko Nozawa
abstract.abstract: Growth is a key demographic process shaping population dynamics by regulating reproduction and mortality, with important consequences for the latitudinal structuring of coral assemblages. Although growth in reef-building corals generally declines with increasing latitude, it remains unclear whether this pattern is consistent across taxa and colony sizes. Here, we test the hypothesis that coral growth responses differ between tropical and subtropical-temperate regions, and these differences are both size-dependent and taxon-specific, reflecting differential environmental constraints and life-history strategies. We quantified annual growth rates for 941 colonies spanning a wide size range (planar tissue area, 0.2–1,904 cm²) from five common coral genera (Acropora, Pocillopora, Porites, Dipsastraea, and Favites) across tropical (7 sites, 5°S–9°N) and subtropical–temperate (7 sites, 26–32°N) regions in the western Pacific from 2012 to 2014. For each genus, we applied linear mixed-effects models to evaluate whether growth differed between latitudinal regions and how it varied with colony size. We found pronounced genus- and size-specific growth patterns across latitudinal regions. Pocillopora and Porites grew faster in the tropical region, with differences decreasing as colony size increased. Acropora showed similar trends but high individual variability obscured significant differences. In contrast, Dipsastraea and Favites exhibited faster growth in the tropical region primarily in juvenile size classes. Our findings challenge the assumption of uniform latitudinal declines in coral growth and demonstrate that growth responses across latitudinal regions depend strongly on both taxon and colony size. Incorporating such variability into demographic models will improve predictions of trajectories and tropicalization in coral assemblages under ongoing climate warming.

items.name: Tomohiro Nakazono
items.title: Resource access in spatially structured nests: Queen-associated areas enhance provisioning by workers to a termite-associated rove beetle

abstract.authors: Tomohiro Nakazono*, Kiyotaka Yabe, Takuya Noro, Mamoru Takata, Kenji Matsuura
abstract.abstract: Social insect colonies are spatially heterogeneous, with castes, activities, and resources distributed unevenly across the nest and thereby creating distinct local social environments. Social parasites acquire host-derived resources within these organized societies, yet most previous studies have emphasized parasite traits or associations with particular host individuals or nest locations. How local social environments influence parasite–host interactions and resource acquisition therefore remains an important question. Here, we investigated the termite-associated rove beetle Trichopsenius japonicus, a social parasite of Reticulitermes speratus. Field surveys showed that beetles were concentrated near termite reproductives in natural nests. In preference assays, beetles occupied chambers containing queens more often than those containing kings or additional workers. Behavioural observations further revealed that queen presence increased beetle begging and provisioning by workers. Together, these results indicate that remaining near queens can enhance opportunities for beetles to obtain resources from workers. More broadly, our findings suggest that resource acquisition by social parasites may depend not only on the host individuals involved, but also on the local social context in which parasite–host interactions take place.

items.name: Chia-Chien Wu
items.title: Elevational shifts in intraspecific body size and mandibular morphology of termites

abstract.authors: Chia-Chien Wu*, Wen-Jun Lin, Hsin-Ting Yeh, Hou-Feng Li
abstract.abstract: Body size is a crucial ecological trait, which could be influenced by elevation. The intraspecific responses and mechanisms which are influenced by elevation in termites remain unclear. Mandibles are the most sclerotized and resource-intensive body parts in termites. It is unknown whether mandibles sustain resource allocation during body size changes under limited resources. In this research, we investigated elevational body size trends and mandibular allometry in four widely distributed termite species in Taiwan: Odontotermes formosanus, Glyptotermes satsumensis, Reticulitermes kanmonensis, and Nasutitermes parvonasutus. The results show that not all species exhibited increased body size with elevation. Shifts in colony mean body size were driven by two potential mechanisms: altered individual sizes within the same instar across environments, or changes in colony instar composition despite constant individual instar sizes. In workers and soldiers of all species, mandibles showed significant negative allometry. However, mandibular growth lacked an asymptote, indicating continuous growth relative to other body parts. During this growth, resource allocation is dynamic; sclerotized volume increases, and the bite force moment of different teeth changes accordingly.

items.name: Riou Mizuno
items.title: The hunting behavior spectrum of the tiny trap-jaw ant Strumigenys: wandering to ambush

abstract.authors: Riou Mizuno*, Nurul Ashikin, Aupanun Sunittra, Yek Sze Huei, Evan P. Economo
abstract.abstract: The ant genus Strumigenys is one of the most diversified ant groups, with nearly 900 described species. Some species have extremely fast trap-jaw that operate on a latch-and-spring mechanism. According to recent molecular phylogeny, this mechanism evolved multiple times among clades distributed across different biogeographic regions. Furthermore, even among these phylogenetically distant species, they exhibit strikingly similar morphologies, suggesting that not only the trap-jaw mechanism but also various related traits have evolved convergently. The most important advantage of the trap-jaw is likely predation, as they are known as predators of agile prey like springtails. Previous studies have suggested that species without a locking mechanism tend to move slowly and have ambush or stalking hunting strategies. In contrast, trap-jaw species with a locking mechanism exhibit more active prey search. However, actual hunting behavior was observed in only a small number of species, and these observations are also phylogenetically biased. To address this knowledge gap, we observed and compared the hunting behavior of trap-jaw Strumigenys species originating from the Oriental and Neotropical regions. As a result, we observed that a few species exhibit extremely passive ambush-hunting behavior previously unknown to trap-jaw species. In addition, we found the species with this ambush-hunting strategy in both Oriental and Neotropical clades.

items.name: Wan-Yi Chen
items.aff: Department of Entomology, National Taiwan University
items.title: Exploring the Physiological Mechanisms Underlying Sublethal Imidacloprid-Induced Early Foraging Behavior in Honey Bee Workers

abstract.authors: Wan-Yi Chen*, En-Cheng Yang
abstract.abstract:
Colony collapse disorder (CCD) of the honey bee, Apis mellifera, is an abnormal phenomenon marked by the sudden loss of most worker bees, including hive bees and foragers, in a colony. Previous studies have shown that exposure to environmental stressors, such as the neonicotinoid pesticide imidacloprid, can trigger early behavioral maturation in hive bees and impair the flight and homing abilities of foragers. These symptoms are closely linked to the rapid collapse of honey bee colonies. The transition from hive tasks to foraging behavior is coordinated with the increasing level of juvenile hormone (JH) III, which plays a crucial role in age polyethism. Elevated levels of JH III in young hive bees can cause early behavioral maturation and result in precocious foraging activity. Despite these insights, the molecular and physiological mechanisms underlying stress-induced precocious forager behavior remain largely unknown, but they may be associated with the level of JH III.  
To investigate the molecular and physiological mechanisms underlying sublethal imidacloprid-induced precocious foraging, we used next-generation sequencing (NGS) and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) to monitor trends in transcriptome profiles and JH III titers in workers of different ages between imidacloprid-treated and control groups. Our initial findings indicate that the transcriptomic profiles of imidacloprid-treated young workers closely resembled those of older control workers, suggesting accelerated behavioral maturation at the molecular level. More frequent sampling from emergence to day 21 revealed age-specific reductions in nurse-associated gene expression and increases in foraging- and JH-associated gene expression. Correspondingly, JH III titers rose earlier in imidacloprid-treated workers, providing physiological evidence consistent with accelerated worker maturation.
The outcome of this project provides genetic and physiological evidence that exposure to sublethal imidacloprid during the larval stage may disrupt the age polyethism in the colony; this could potentially impair individual bee development and threaten colony stability. Our results highlight the need for further research into the long-term ecological impacts of neonicotinoid exposure on honey bee populations.

items.name: Ching-Chen Lee
items.title: What we know so far about the invasive yellow crazy ant, Anoplolepis gracilipes (Hymenoptera: Formicidae): From trophic egg production to management

abstract.authors: Ching-Chen Lee*, Jia-Wei Tay, Fuminori Ito, Chin-Cheng Scotty Yang, Chung-Chi Lin
abstract.abstract: The yellow crazy ant, Anoplolepis gracilipes, is a globally destructive invasive species due to its substantial impacts on biological diversity and ecosystem sustainability. In Taiwan, invasion of A. gracilipes has been associated with declines in land crab populations at several hotspots, and liquid baiting has been implemented since 2018. A better understanding of its biology, behavior and reproduction mode may provide new insights into the development of future pest management strategies. First, a generalized additive model indicated that worker abundance was associated with the human disturbance levels, suggesting that habitat restoration coupled with the removal of human-made objects that may serve as nesting sites for A. gracilipes could discourage its establishment. Moreover, deployment of artificial nests or trapping boxes in areas with high ant activity may facilitate the removal of entire functional colonies. Field studies showed that a single artificial nest successfully removed thousand of workers along with substantial brood and queens from surrounding environments. Second, multidisciplinary approaches revealed that a subset of A. gracilipes workers possess greatly distended gaster and functional ovaries (i.e., physogastric workers).  Physogastric workers are an essential worker subcaste as they produce trophic eggs that constitute a major food source for larvae. Therefore, incorporating a low concentration of juvenile hormone analogue as an active ingredient in bait may disrupt the nutrition supply for larvae and subsequently inhibit colony growth. Third, field assay indicated that A. gracilipes workers preferentially retrieved small-size hydrogel beads (outer diameter = 3.1 mm), which could be readily carried by workers and transported directly back to the nest. The deployment of small hydrogel beads may therefore facilitate the efficient transfer of toxicant within the colony while maintaining the palatability of liquid bait over extended periods. Collectively, these findings support an integrated approach to the sustainable management of A. gracilipes.

items.name: Juchieh Wu
items.title: Spatial Facilitation as Biotic Response to Chronic Wind Stress in Cloud Forest Communities

abstract.authors: Juchieh Wu*, David Zelený
abstract.abstract:
Chronic wind stress is a major physical driver shaping tree interactions. The Stress-Gradient Hypothesis (SGH) predicts that plant interactions shift from competition to facilitation under extreme stress. However, models often assume these interactions are symmetric, leaving the role of functional traits unclear. To investigate this, 5-year tree growth dynamics were analyzed across a continuous, monsoon-driven wind gradient in a subtropical montane cloud forest. Spatial interactions were evaluated using a spatial model and the Neighborhood Competition Index (NCI), incorporating local wind exposure and differences in Specific Leaf Area (SLA) between target trees and neighbors.

A directional shift toward facilitation was observed under high wind exposure, supporting the SGH. Sheltering effects occurred specifically when conservative neighbors (low SLA) buffered resource-acquisitive target trees (high SLA) against wind stress. This physical shielding provided by conservative neighbors mitigates mechanical damage, offsetting the costs of local resource competition. The results demonstrate that the stress gradient hypothesis manifest only if considering the functional strategies between neighbors and target individuals in the forest.

items.name: Yan-Han Wu
items.title: Fog Frequency Promotes Functional Trait Diversity in Montane Cloud Forests of Northern Taiwan

abstract.authors: Yan-Han Wu*, Shu-I Lin, and David Zelený
abstract.abstract: Montane cloud forests (MCFs) are rare and fragile ecosystems in Taiwan, strongly shaped by typhoons, monsoons, and frequent fog. This study explores how fog frequency influences functional trait diversity in northern Taiwan’s MCFs. Using 27 transect plots along a fog gradient, we calculated functional richness, dispersion, and evenness using individual-level data for seven plant traits. Linear regressions were used to test the relationships between fog frequency and these diversity indices. Results indicate that foggier sites exhibit significantly higher functional richness and dispersion. However, the relationship between fog frequency and functional evenness is non-significant. As a stressful environmental factor, fog creates cold, humid climate. Surprisingly, instead of homogenizing plant traits, foggier sites show significant functional differentiation. This study offers new ecological interpretations of fog effect on cloud forest vegetation, providing valuable insights for understanding how MCFs function and better understanding how to conserve them.

items.name: Bo-Moon Kim
items.aff: Department of Biological Sciences, Tokyo Metropolitan University
items.title: Dispersal Modulates the Effects of Kin Recognition on Biodiversity

abstract.authors: Bo-Moon Kim*, Akira Yamawo, Yuuya Tachiki
abstract.abstract:
Kin recognition has been documented in numerous plant species; however, its ecological consequences at the community level remain poorly understood. In particular, how kin recognition (genotype discrimination) among neighboring plants influences long-term species coexistence under different dispersal regimes remains unclear. Here, we developed an individual-based simulation model to investigate how kin recognition-mediated cooperation affects biodiversity in spatially structured plant communities.
The model simulated clonal perennial plants on a two-dimensional triangular lattice, where individuals discriminated neighbors based on species identity and pedigree relatedness. Fitness modifications occurred when two related conspecifics interacted with one heterospecific. We compared two cooperation scenarios: a Zero-sum scenario, in which cooperation redistributed fitness without increasing total productivity, and a Tragedy of the Commons (ToC) scenario, in which cooperation generated additional fitness benefits. Both scenarios were examined under local and global dispersal.
Species diversity was consistently higher under local than global dispersal. Local dispersal preserved spatial kin structure, allowing repeated interactions among related individuals and strengthening kin recognition-mediated cooperation. Species persistence increased particularly in the ToC scenario. In contrast, global dispersal disrupted local kin structure and reduced the influence of kin recognition.
Our results demonstrate that the ecological consequences of kin recognition depend on dispersal mode. Kin recognition alone is insufficient to maintain biodiversity; its benefits emerge when restricted dispersal preserves local kin structure. Thus, limited seed dispersal may be a key condition under which kin recognition-mediated cooperation contributes to long-term species coexistence and community stability.

items.name: Chang-Yu Chang
items.title: Decomposing Symbiotic Trait Variation: Dependence on Host Evolution

abstract.authors: Chang-Yu Chang* and Corlett Wood
abstract.abstract: How is symbiotic trait variation partitioned across host evolutionary scales? Using a structured block design, we evaluated multi-trait distributions across 1,004 live host plants to quantify how variance is distributed between versus within host species. We tracked functional traits across shoot biomass, root architecture, and symbiotic organ structures (nodules and galls). Using Bayesian mixed-effects models, we calculated model goodness-of-fit and decomposed latent phenotypic variance into host species phylogeny, interspecies variation, intraspecies variation, and experimental block effects. We show that the influence of host evolutionary history varies substantially across trait types: symbiotic organ variation is primarily driven by within-species differences, whereas whole-plant performance metrics are dominated by between-species variation. These results demonstrate how host phylogeny differentially structures phenotypic outcomes in plant-microbe symbioses across macro- and micro-evolutionary scales.

items.name: Chao-Li Huang
items.title: Harnessing the "Earth’s Breath": Translating Plant-Microbiome Negotiations in Pine Evolution

abstract.authors: Yan-Han Fang, Yen-Ju Chen, Hsin-Ni Liu, Chao-Li Huang*
abstract.abstract: In traditional Chinese philosophy, "Earth's Breath" describes the land's vital energy flow. Biologically, this manifests as plant-soil feedbacks driven by cellular oxidative metabolism across the electron transport chains, gradually converting organic matter into mineral nutrients. Unlike the gentle energy flow of decomposition, wildfires represent an unruly oxidation. Traditionally, plants are viewed as passive, while we hypothesized that plants are active holobionts that dynamically guide microbial functions to regulate Earth's Breath. Fire-avoiding pines (Pinus morrisonicola) promote rapid decomposition and robust nitrogen cycling, sustaining their nutrients by continuously flowing with Earth's Breath. In contrast, fire-tolerant pines (P. taiwanensis) may intentionally suppress soil decomposition, effectively holding Earth's Breath to await the massive nutrient release of a post-wildfire reset. We hypothesize pines evolved to either flow with or suppress this energy. Through shotgun metagenomics, we may monitor these underground energetic states, providing cues for building a climate-resilient ecosystem.

items.name: Koki Katsuhara
items.title: Urbanised landscape and microhabitat differences can influence flowering phenology and synchrony in an annual herb

abstract.authors: *Koki Katsuhara, Hinata Fujiwara, Hiroto Yamaguchi, Kazuyoshi Nakata
abstract.abstract:
Flowering phenology is sensitive to human impacts, such as climate change and urbanisation. Numerous studies have examined how urbanised landscapes affect flowering phenology, by comparing along urban–rural gradients. Phenological patterns among microenvironments in the urban ecosystem have received less attention, even though they often offer unique habitats with varying degrees of artificial influence, such as roadsides, drainage ditches, and vacant lots. If microenvironmental differences diversify flowering phenology, the urban matrix might reduce flowering synchrony with neighbouring populations, limiting outcrossing opportunities and therefore reducing reproductive success.
We investigated the flowering phenology and synchrony of the native annual herb Commelina communis in approximately 250 populations at two rural and two urban sites over three years. Our findings revealed that populations in urban sites exhibited earlier flowering onset compared to populations in rural sites. For flowering synchrony, we found that the population in urban sites, growing in drain habitats, and with artificial disturbances, exhibited relatively lower interpopulation flowering synchrony, suggesting their phenology differed from neighbouring populations within the same landscape. These findings highlight the need to consider not only spatial but also temporal fragmentation from diversified flowering phenology when addressing conservation in the urban matrix.

items.name: Chun-Wen Yang
items.aff: Institute of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, National Taiwan University
items.title: University campuses as model systems for understanding species-specific responses of frogs to urban landscapes

abstract.authors: Chun-Wen Yang* and Da-Li Lin
abstract.abstract: Urban expansion has become one of the most pressing global environmental challenges, increasing the need to design biodiversity-friendly cities. However, the complex stakeholder relationships of urban areas make it difficult to be realised. University campuses provide an ideal model system because they represent simplified urban environments that contain both built infrastructure, semi-natural habitats, and high human density. We used university campuses as a microcosm of urban areas to investigate how land cover types influences frog communities. We applied generalized linear mixed models with an information-theoretic model selection framework to examine the associations of frog diversity and land cover types on the campuses. The results show that road coverage consistently received the strongest model support and was negatively associated with frog species richness and several widespread frog species. In contrast, forest, farmland, and water coverage generally exhibited lower support and species-specific effects, indicating that different frog species respond differently to campus land cover composition. Our findings present that university campuses could serve as practical model systems for understanding urban biodiversity. Although amphibian responses to landscape composition are highly species-specific, reducing road impacts should be prioritised in biodiversity-friendly campus planning. These results also provide a scientific basis for extending campus-scale conservation strategies to broader urban planning and green infrastructure design.

items.name: Man-Lin Lin
items.aff: Institute of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, National Taiwan University
items.title: Road mortality of snake across heterogeneous landscapes in subtropical Asia

abstract.authors: MAN-LIN, LIN* , DA-LI, LIN
abstract.abstract: Roadkill is a major source of wildlife mortality worldwide, and snakes are particularly vulnerable due to their movement behavior and frequent use of roads. However, the influence of landscape structure on snake roadkill remains poorly understood. We examined species-specific associations between landscape structure and roadkill using 13,288 records of 24 snake species collected through a nationwide citizen science project in Taiwan from 2013 to 2017. Generalized linear mixed models were used to evaluate the effects of landscape compositional heterogeneity, configurational heterogeneity, and habitat amount on roadkill counts. Roadkill counts of four species, *Bungarus multicinctus*, *Psammodynastes pulverulentus*, *Oreocryptophis porphyraceus*, and *Elaphe taeniura*, were significantly associated with landscape compositional heterogeneity, whereas configurational heterogeneity showed no significant effects. Regarding habitat amount, roadkill counts of *Naja atra*, *P. pulverulentus*, and *Ptyas mucosa* were significantly negatively associated with forest cover, while *Ptyas major* showed a significant positive association with farmland cover. These results suggest that landscape compositional heterogeneity may be more important than habitat configuration in explaining snake roadkill risk, while habitat effects vary among species. Our findings highlight strong species-specific responses and emphasize the importance of incorporating landscape characteristics into road planning and wildlife mitigation strategies.

items.name: Po-An Lin
items.title: How does news of herbivore attack travel through a field of plants?

abstract.authors: Wan-Yi Liao, Matthias Erb, Po-An Lin*
abstract.abstract: Plants use airborne volatiles to coordinate defence, yet environmental stress may alter both signal production and how exposed neighbours relay information. Using maize under well-watered, 2-day drought and 5-day drought treatments, we combined PTR-MS and GC-MS with emitter–receiver assays and an empirically constrained spatial simulation. Water limitation changed the strength and composition of indole-rich herbivore-induced plant volatile sources without abolishing induced emission. Receiver-associated indole output varied with the water status of both emitter and receiver plants. In the 5-day trial, the stronger source from well-watered emitters produced lower receiver output than the weaker drought-derived source, whereas 2-day drought receivers responded positively to both sources. In the simulated stand, measured receiver responses extended volatile signal transmission beyond passive transport, and modelled transmission occurred under every tested water-status combination. These findings show that water availability reorganizes airborne defence information at both the emission and receiver stages.

items.name: Chih-Chieh Yu
items.title: Contrasting biogeographic histories of montane plant lineages in Taiwan and the Japanese Archipelago

abstract.authors: Chih-Chieh Yu*
abstract.abstract: Mountain environments in Taiwan and the Japanese Archipelago harbor exceptionally high levels of plant endemism, yet the biogeographic origins of these montane floras remain poorly understood. The two regions differ markedly in latitude, island age, and orogenic history, providing a striking contrast in their natural histories. We therefore expect that their alpine floras have followed distinct histories of assembly and diversification. In this study, we selected several alpine plant lineages distributed predominantly across the Northern Hemisphere and integrated publicly available sequence data with newly generated data to reconstruct their phylogenetic and historical biogeographic patterns. We further applied biogeographic stochastic mapping to reconstruct the potential histories of dispersal, vicariance, and extinction experienced by these lineages in Taiwan, Honshu, and Hokkaido, while accounting for uncertainty in phylogenetic relationships and ancestral range estimation. We then compared temporal changes in these biogeographic processes to investigate how geographic and biological factors have jointly shaped the assembly of alpine floras across these regions. By doing this, our study will help elucidate the biogeographic processes underlying the rich and highly endemic plant diversity of the western Pacific montane islands.

items.name: Tosuke Sakagami
items.title: Convergent evolution of animal photosymbiosis through co-option of an ancestral endodermal program revealed in acoels

abstract.authors: Sakagami T*, Kao LJ, Su JY, Lewin TD, Wen SH, Piñon-Gonzalez VM, Chiu YL, Wu MY, Arimoto A, Tagawa K, Lu TM, Luo YJ
abstract.abstract: Photosymbiosis has evolved independently across multiple animal phyla, yet the cellular principles that repeatedly enabled animals to accommodate photosynthetic symbionts remain unknown. Here we show that the acoel Praesagittifera naikaiensis establishes intercellular photosymbiosis through division of labour among conserved endodermal cell populations rather than the evolution of a specialised symbiont-hosting cell type. Combining single-cell transcriptomics with perturbation of symbiont photosynthesis, we identify an endodermal transcriptional program underlying symbiont maintenance. Lineage-specific genes associated with photosymbiosis are recruited into this endodermal program. Comparative analyses reveal that independently evolved photosymbioses in acoels, corals and sponges converge on the same ancestral endodermal program despite fundamentally distinct cellular architectures and symbiont localisation strategies. Endodermal cells are enriched for evolutionarily ancient metabolic functions and exhibit elevated transcriptional plasticity, suggesting that they provide a conserved cellular context predisposed to regulatory rewiring and symbiont accommodation. Together, our findings suggest that repeated origins of animal photosymbiosis were enabled through recurrent co-option of an ancestral endodermal program coupled with lineage-specific innovations, revealing a general cellular principle underlying the convergent evolution of complex symbioses.

items.name: Taiga Uchida
items.aff: Atmosphere and Ocean Research Institute, The University of Tokyo
items.title: Genomic insights into the mechanisms and evolution of extracellular photosymbiosis in giant clams

abstract.authors: Taiga Uchida*, Hiroshi Yamashita, Go Shimada, Mayumi Kawamitsu, Eiichi Shoguchi, Chuya Shinzato
abstract.abstract:
Giant clams are iconic bivalves of coral reef ecosystems that harbor photosynthetic symbionts of the family Symbiodiniaceae. Unlike reef-building corals, which maintain their symbionts intracellularly, giant clams host algal cells extracellularly within a tubular system in the outer mantle. However, the molecular mechanisms and evolutionary basis of this unusual photosymbiosis remain poorly understood.
Here, we generated a chromosome-scale genome of the boring giant clam Tridacna crocea and combined comparative genomics with tissue-specific transcriptomics and dark-induced bleaching experiments to identify host genes associated with symbiosis. These analyses revealed several candidate genes potentially involved in nutrient exchange and maintenance of the symbiotic relationship. Among them, genes related to inorganic nitrogen transport may contribute to nutrient supply to the symbiotic algae, while other candidates suggest molecular features shared with intracellular photosymbioses in cnidarians. Comparative and phylogenetic analyses further provided insights into the evolutionary history of these symbiosis-related genes. Together, our results suggest that both conserved and distinctive molecular features may have contributed to the evolution of giant clam photosymbiosis.

items.name: Kamal Md Mostafa
items.aff: Institute of Molecular Biology, Academia Sinica
items.title: Host lipid remodeling and fatty-acid carbon transfer in the Paramecium bursaria–Chlorella photosymbiosis

abstract.authors: Yan-Jun Chen, Chi-Yen Wei, Chia-Wei Hsu, Pei-Ling Wang, Silver Sung-Yun Hsiao, Der-Chuen Lee, Chia-Ling Yang, Chuan Ku, Chuan-Chih Hsu, Md Mostafa Kamal*, and Jun-Yi Leu
abstract.abstract: Photosymbioses are usually viewed as partnerships in which algal symbionts provide photosynthetically fixed carbon to heterotrophic hosts, while hosts provide nutrients and intracellular habitat. Using the ciliate Paramecium bursaria and its green algal symbiont Chlorella variabilis, we investigated how host cellular organization and lipid metabolism contribute to the maintenance of this endosymbiosis. Spatial proteomics of symbiotic and aposymbiotic P. bursaria mapped host proteins across subcellular compartments, identified a candidate perialgal vacuole-associated protein signature, and revealed pronounced remodeling of host lipid droplets during symbiosis. Imaging and pharmacological perturbation showed that lipid droplets accumulate near intracellular algae and that disruption of host lipid metabolism reduces endosymbiont abundance. We then tested whether these remodeled lipid pools participate in metabolic exchange. Lipidomics showed extensive lipid remodeling in both host lipid droplets and endosymbiotic algae. Stable-isotope tracing with host-supplied 13C-oleic acid, combined with NanoSIMS, EA-IRMS, and isotopologue-resolved lipidomics, demonstrated that host-acquired fatty-acid carbon reaches intracellular algae and is incorporated into algal storage and membrane lipids. These results reveal host-to-symbiont organic-carbon transfer and broaden the conventional view of carbon exchange in photosymbiosis.

items.name: Takumi Yokomizo
items.aff: Center for Ecological Research, Kyoto University
items.title: Plasticity of biological rhythms underlying the colonization of tidal environments in a freshwater snail

abstract.authors: *Takumi Yokomizo, Yuma Takahashi
abstract.abstract: Synchronization with environmental cycles is fundamental for adaptation to rhythmic environments. In a river, water level fluctuations of a 12.4-hour period induced by tidal cycles become more pronounced further downstream. Consequently, biological rhythms may be modified during colonization of non-tidal to tidal habitats. This study analyzed the activity and transcriptomic rhythms in tidal and non-tidal populations of the freshwater snail Semisulcospira reiniana. Under field and laboratory constant conditions, snails in the non-tidal population exhibited diurnal activity patterns, whereas those in the tidal population displayed tidal activity rhythms. The number of genes with tidal rhythmic expression under constant conditions was greater in the tidal population than in the non-tidal population. These results suggest that snails in the tidal population possess biological rhythms with a 12.4-hour period (i.e., circatidal rhythm). The snails were then exposed to simulated tidal cycles to examine the plasticity of their biological rhythms. In both populations, snails exposed to tidal cycles exhibited circatidal activity rhythms and increased tidal rhythmic genes under constant conditions; however, tidal rhythmic genes were more abundant in the tidal populations under comparable conditions. These findings suggest that differences in the rhythms of wild populations result from environmental factors and evolutionary changes during tidal colonization.
abstract.affiliation: Center for Ecological Research, Kyoto University

items.name: Takamasa Yoneyama
items.title: Morphological adaptation of the filter screen in Daphnia under low-nutrient conditions

abstract.authors:
*Takamasa Yoneyama<sup>1</sup>, Masaki Sakamoto<sup>2</sup>, Hitoshi Miyakawa<sup>1</sup>
<sup>1</sup>Utsunomiya University, Japan
<sup>2</sup>Toyama Prefectural University, Japan
abstract.abstract: Starvation is one of the most serious constraint on somatic growth in animals. It can be particularly critical for arthropods with short life cycles. Under food-limited conditions, animals generally reduce investment in growth and development. In contrast, the herbivorous zooplankton Daphnia enlarge the filter screens on their thoracic limbs in response to food shortage. This response is physiologically intriguing because Daphnia invest in the development of their feeding structures despite limited nutrient availability. Our previous ecological research has shown that the degree of filter-screen enlargement differed between clones, suggesting a genetic basis for variation in this morphological plasticity. However, the developmental and cellular mechanisms underlying this morphological response are unclear. Furthermore, the genetic variants causing morphological adaptability between clones have not been identified. The aim of the present study is to elucidate the developmental and cellular mechanisms that regulate the filter-screen enlargement. To this end, cytological observations were initially conducted to determine the developmental stage at which enlargement of the filtering screen occurs. The distribution of cell nuclei in the thoracic limbs was observed using DAPI staining.

items.name: Natsumi Maruoka
items.title: Ecological significance and molecular basis of variation in diapause strategies in natural Daphnia populations

abstract.authors: Natsumi Maruoka*, Hitoshi Miyakawa
abstract.abstract: Diapause enables organisms to survive unfavorable conditions. Although cues such as photoperiod and crowding induce diapause, its propensity varies within species, contributing to adaptation to diverse habitats. However, the molecular basis of this variation remains poorly understood. The water flea Daphnia produces resting eggs as a diapause stage. We investigated the ecological significance and molecular basis of diapause strategies in asexual Daphnia cf. pulex. Field surveys and laboratory experiments revealed that, among two coexisting lineages in the same lake, the lineage with a lower population growth rate rapidly produced resting eggs as competitor density increased. This may allow production of resting eggs before being competitively excluded, suggesting that differences in diapause strategies contribute to their coexistence. To uncover the molecular basis of these differences, we established a comparative system in which resting eggs were consistently induced only in the diapause-prone lineage. Transcriptomic analysis identified genes whose expression changed prior to resting-egg production and implicated juvenile hormone (JH) signaling. Subsequent experiments demonstrated that JH induces resting-egg production and that JH responsiveness differed between lineages with contrasting diapause strategies. Thus, variation in diapause strategies is associated with differences in JH responsiveness. We are currently using genome editing to elucidate this pathway.

items.name: Lily Cheng Clavel
items.title: Interactions between understory cover and the negative dependence of conspecific density on tree seedling dynamics: the roles of shade tolerance and mycorrhizal type

abstract.authors:
Lily Cheng Clavel*, Chia-Hsiu Tsai, Jiun-Nan Huang, Po-Hui Chiang,
Po-Ju Ke, Chia-Hao Chang-Yang
abstract.abstract:
Conspecific negative density dependence (CNDD) and understory vegetation are important drivers of forest regeneration, yet their combined effects on seedling performance remain poorly understood. We investigated how neighboring tree identity and understory vegetation affect seedling growth and survival in two dominant subtropical rainforest species, in northeastern Taiwan. Seedlings were planted beneath conspecific or heterospecific adult trees with or without understory removal, and a complementary experiment tested the effects of seedling density on performance.
Understory removal consistently enhanced seedling performance. For Engelhardia roxburghiana, removal increased both growth and survival, particularly during the first 400 days, whereas Machilus zuihoensis showed significantly higher survival and a marginal increase in growth. Neighboring tree identity significantly affected seedling survival in both species but had weak effects on growth, with M. zuihoensis surviving better beneath heterospecific than conspecific neighbors during the first 400 days. Seedling density had no significant effect on growth or survival in either species.
Our results indicate that seedling regeneration in the Fushan subtropical forest is jointly shaped by understory vegetation and neighboring tree identity. Contrasting species responses suggest that shade tolerance and mycorrhizal associations may drive species-specific regeneration patterns, underscoring the importance of biotic neighborhood effects for forest management and restoration.

items.title: Frugivory set the stage: genomic and physiological changes underlying a sexually selected bird radiation

abstract.authors: Christopher N. Balakrishnan, Yasuka Toda, Meng-Ching Ko*, Morgan E. Wirthlin, Robert J. Driver, Peri E. Bolton, Eliot T. Miller, Daniel Mendez-Aranda, Rebecca B. Dikow, Paul B. Friedrich, Camilo Alfonso Cuta, James B. Pease, Alexander A. Nevue, Chad Tomlinson, Aleksey Zimin, Matthew I.M. Louder, Michael S. Brewer, Rachael A. Bay, Kristen Ruegg, Thomas B. Smith, Yoshiro Ishimaru, Andreas R. Pfenning, Carolina Frankl-Vilches, Manfred Gahr, Claudio V. Mello, Rebecca T. Kimball, Edward L. Braun, John G. Blake, Lainy B. Day, T. Brandt Ryder, Ignacio T. Moore, Brent M. Horton, Barney A. Schlinger, Matthew J. Fuxjager, Wesley C. Warren, Emily H. DuVal, W. Alice Boyle, Bette A. Loiselle, Michael J. Braun, Maude W. Baldwin
abstract.abstract: Sexual selection varies enormously in strength across animals, yet why certain lineages evolve extraordinary ornaments and displays remains unclear. Strikingly, several of the bird families with the most elaborate plumage and courtship — birds of paradise, cotingas and manakins — are also specialist frugivores, hinting that dietary and mating-system evolution are linked. We tested this connection in manakins (Pipridae), a Neotropical radiation famous for acrobatic lek displays, combining new genome assemblies with functional assays and comparative phylogenetics. All manakin genomes show Z-to-autosome diversity ratios well below the neutral expectation of 0.75, a predicted signature of the strong reproductive skew of lekking, whereas monogamous outgroups do not. Scans for positive selection highlight genes for muscle function, visual perception and dietary physiology, with protein digestion and absorption the only enriched functional category. Two candidates were tested functionally: the umami receptor T1R1–T1R3, which we show acquired sugar sensing at the base of Pipridae through substitutions concentrated in T1R3, and lactase-phlorizin hydrolase, whose glycoside-hydrolysing activity was reduced earlier, in the Tyrannida ancestor. These physiological changes preceded shifts in breeding system and the evolution of dichromatic plumage, suggesting that intensified frugivory set the stage for one of the planet's most colourful and acrobatic avian radiations.
