items.name: Mari Esashi
items.title: Do Hosts and Parasites Share the Same History? Comparative Phylogeography of a Scops Owl and Its Bird-Parasitic Fly across Japan and Taiwan

abstract.authors: Mari ESASHI* and Tomoki HIROSE
abstract.abstract: Geographic isolation of islands can leave strong signatures in the genomes of both hosts and their parasites. However, host and parasite may experience very different opportunities for dispersal, potentially resulting in contrasting phylogeographic histories. Here, we investigate this question using the Scops Owl species (Otus semitorques and O. lettia) and their ectoparasitic fly, Carnus orientalis, across Japan and Taiwan. We analyzed genome-wide SNPs generated by MIG-seq and mitochondrial COI sequences from Japanese populations of the owl, together with publicly available COI sequences from a closely related Taiwanese population. For C. orientalis, we analyzed COI sequences from Okinawa, Ishikawa, and Sado in Japan and compared them with sequences from Taiwan. Preliminary results indicate strong geographic differentiation in the parasite, with each island forming a genetically distinct group. Phylogenetic relationships of the host and parasite will be compared to assess the degree of geographic and evolutionary concordance between them. We ask whether the parasite has followed the evolutionary history of its host, or whether its distribution reflects independent dispersal and colonization. By comparing these two interacting organisms across the Japan–Taiwan region, this study explores how island geography and host association jointly shape the evolutionary histories of host–parasite systems.

items.name: Jui-Hung Tai
items.title: Repeated introductions and asymmetric reproductive interference threaten native freshwater fishes in Taiwan

abstract.authors: Jui-Hung Tai*, Chen-Fan Wang, Tzi-Yuan Wang, Hurng-Yi Wang
abstract.abstract: Understanding how introduced species establish populations and affect native species is a central issue in invasion biology. Here, we combined whole-genome analyses, demographic inference, hybrid identification, published survey data, and simulations to investigate the introduction history of Zacco platypus in Taiwan and its potential ecological impacts. Genomic data show that Taiwanese Z. platypus comprise two distinct genomic clusters associated with the Keelung and Xindian rivers. Demographic analyses supported independent introductions of the two populations, each founded by a small number of individuals and followed by rapid population expansion. Genome-wide analyses further confirmed F1 hybridization between Z. platypus and three native Opsariichthyini species. Hybridization with Opsariichthys evolans was strongly asymmetric, with native females serving as the maternal parent in most hybrids, suggesting reproductive costs on native populations. Simulation showed that asymmetric hybridization alone could generate a progressive decline in O. evolans and, under some simulated scenarios, ultimately lead to its replacement by Z. platypus. Consistent with this prediction published survey data revealed declines in the relative abundance of O. evolans in both rivers. Together, our findings reveal multiple independent introductions of Z. platypus in Taiwan and suggest that asymmetric reproductive interference may represent an important mechanism affecting native fish populations.

items.name: Shih-Fan Chan
items.title: The evolution of conditional cooperation: divergent response rules in two burying beetle populations

abstract.authors: Shih-Fan Chan*, Chung-Fan Chang, Dustin R. Rubenstein, Shi-Ping Huang, Mark Liu, Ying-Yu Chen, Shiun-Cheng Chan, Sheng-Feng Shen
abstract.abstract: How much individuals invest in cooperation in animal societies usually remains conditional on the environment, yet why populations differ in this conditionality is largely unknown. We combine a common garden experiment, field manipulations and theoretical modeling to ask whether two populations of the burying beetle Nicrophorus nepalensis diverge in these response rules. In the common garden, offspring from Mt. Hehuan in Taiwan responded more strongly to both blowflies and warming, whereas those from Mt. Jiajin in China showed a much smaller blowfly-induced increase and a weaker temperature response. The populations therefore differ in the conditionality of cooperation rather than in how cooperative they are. In the field, the advantage of groups over pairs increased with temperature at Mt. Hehuan but was confined to the cold end at Mt. Jiajin. That cold end is also where the congener competitor N. schawalleri occurs, absent from Mt. Hehuan. Adding this congener to groups reduced investment and breeding success, indicating that benefits generated by cooperation are hard to retain. The favored rule thus depends on what a cue predicts about the loss cooperation can recover and retain, making cooperative conditionality a distinct axis of social evolution shaped by competitor communities.

items.name: Chen-Ying Kuo
items.title: Social information outweighs resource quality in roost-site selection by disk-winged bats

abstract.authors: Vargas-López, Luis D.; Gómez-Feuillet, Luisa F.; Chen-Ying, Ukea Kuo*; Chaverri, Gloriana
abstract.abstract: Animals use personal and social information when deciding where to feed, reproduce, and rest, but these information sources may conflict. We tested whether social information outweighs resource quality during roost selection in *Thyroptera tricolor*, a social bat that roosts in ephemeral furled leaves. Flying bats were given a choice between an unoccupied high-quality roost and a low-quality roost occupied by a social group member, with social information conveyed through contact calls. We recorded roost choice, entry latency, and response-call timing. Without social information, bats showed no clear preference between roost types. However, when response calls came from the occupied low-quality roost, bats were approximately 40 times more likely to select it despite the availability of a higher-quality alternative. Bats also entered roosts faster when occupants responded quickly, indicating that social cues influenced both choice and decision speed. These findings demonstrate that *T. tricolor* prioritizes social information over resource quality when the two conflict. The benefits of maintaining social cohesion may therefore outweigh the immediate advantages of selecting the highest-quality resource, highlighting how animals integrate competing information sources under ecological uncertainty.

items.name: Hung-Chia Chang
items.aff: Department of Life Science, National Taiwan Normal University
items.title: Does stress change their handedness? Behavioral lateralization in the Northern snake-necked turtle

abstract.authors:
Hung-Chia Chang*, Si-Min Lin
School of Life Science, National Taiwan Normal University, Taipei, Taiwan
abstract.abstract:
Behavioral lateralization has been documented in various animal species and has been proposed as a potential indicator of physiological state and animal welfare. However, evidence for stress-related effects on lateralization in reptiles remains limited. We investigated behavioral lateralization in relation to stress-related behavioral contexts and body condition in twelve Northern snake-necked turtles (𝘊𝘩𝘦𝘭𝘰𝘥𝘪𝘯𝘢 𝘳𝘶𝘨𝘰𝘴𝘢), a species characterized by asymmetric neck bending. Four behavioral assays were conducted: resting posture and feeding handedness represented non-stress contexts, whereas stimulation response and righting reflex represented acute stress-related contexts. Only one individual exhibited significant lateralization, showing a left-biased neck-bending response during the stimulation assay. No significant population-level lateralization was detected in any behavioral assay, although resting behavior showed a marginal trend toward right-biased lateralization. However, lateralization strength was significantly influenced by an interaction between body condition and behavioral context. Low-condition individuals exhibited stronger lateralization under acute stress-related contexts than those in high body condition, and stronger lateralization during stress-related than non-stress behaviors. These findings suggest that behavioral lateralization is generally weak in study turtles, but its expression may vary with body condition and behavioral context. Our results suggest that behavioral lateralization may have potential as a non-invasive indicator of individual physiological condition in reptiles.

Keywords: behavioral lateralization; body condition; handedness; reptiles; stress

items.name: Wei Chen
items.aff: Institute of Oceanography, National Taiwan University
items.title: Stoichiometric imbalance affects competitive superiority in marine herbivorous zooplankton communities

abstract.authors: Wei Chen*, Chih-hao Hsieh, Chia-Ting Chen, Pei-Ling Wang, Pei-Chi Ho
abstract.abstract: Traditionally, abiotic drivers and predator–prey interactions have been considered critical to shaping the species composition of a marine zooplankton community, whereas the role of indirect biotic processes, such as exploitative competition, remains unexamined. The competitive performance of a zooplankton can be limited by biochemical mismatches between its requirements and available prey, known as stoichiometric imbalance. Such imbalance impairs zooplankton growth and reproduction, thereby reducing their competitiveness. Stoichiometric imbalance is known to shape zooplankton communities in freshwater systems; however, its role in marine systems has largely been examined only at species or individual level under experimental conditions. To fill the gap, we measured family-level taxonomic composition and carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus ratios (C:N:P) of herbivorous zooplankton and their stoichiometric imbalance with prey in the southern East China Sea. Our results showed zooplankton stoichiometry was stable within but variable among families. Family-level relative abundance was significantly associated to phosphorus imbalance. Despite seasonal shifts in dominant families, the imbalance–relative abundance relationship remained consistent, suggesting that stoichiometric imbalance is an important factor contributing to which families can dominate. Notably, phosphorus excess did not negatively affect relative abundance, a pattern that contrasts with the traditional stoichiometric knife-edge hypothesis.

items.name: Pin-Yi Chen
items.aff: Institute of Oceanography, National Taiwan University
items.title: Trophic strategies of nanoplankton across environmental gradients

abstract.authors: Pin-Yi Chen*, Wei-Ting Chen, Feng-Hsun Chang & Yi-Chun Yeh
abstract.abstract: Nanoplankton encompass autotrophic, mixotrophic, and heterotrophic taxa that occupy distinct ecological roles in marine food webs, yet how these trophic groups are distributed across environmental gradients remains poorly understood. This study quantified their abundances and evaluated their relationships with environmental gradients in the southern East China Sea. Trophic groups were characterized using a double-staining protocol and a CytoSense flow cytometer. Principal component analysis (PCA) revealed distinct horizontal (shelf – offshore) and vertical sample distributions driven by environmental parameters and nanoplankton abundances. Mixotrophic nanoplankton abundance was marginally correlated with salinity and temperature, consistent with previous studies showing that their distribution is governed by water masses. Heterotrophic nanoplankton abundance was negatively correlated with relative mixed-layer depth (Z / Z_MLD). In contrast, expected environmental drivers, including light availability for autotrophs, showed no significant correlation with the abundance of individual trophic groups, suggesting that strong vertical mixing may weaken the coupling between trophic group distributions and conventional environmental controls, such as light limitation. These findings provide empirical insight into nanoplankton trophic dynamics under well-mixed hydrodynamic conditions.

items.name: Shi-Rong Su
items.title: Coupling the Dilution Method and Stable Isotope Analysis to Investigate Trophic Structure and Energy Flow in Planktonic Food Webs

abstract.authors: Shi-Rong Su *、Feng-Hsun Chang
abstract.abstract:
Many studies have shown that microbial food webs dominate more than 70% of carbon cycling in the ocean, particularly through the trophic interactions among pico- and nano-sized plankton. Trophic interactions among pico- and nanoplankton are commonly inferred from their isotopic signatures. However, the complex trophic relationship may blur such isotopic signatures. The objective of this study is to assess this potential mismatch by confronting the empirically measured isotopic signatures and trophic interactions.
In this study, dilution experiments were conducted to estimate isotopic signatures as the growth rates and grazing mortality of pico- and nanoplankton. Size-fractionated filtration was used to separate pico- and nano-sized particulate organic matter (POM) for measuring carbon and nitrogen stable isotope signature (δ¹³C and δ¹⁵N). We have conducted dilution experiments and isotope sampling across marine environments including rocky coast, estuarine, and open ocean. The ultimate goal of this study is to establish a relationship between trophic interactions and carbon and nitrogen stable isotope signatures across different water masses and to provide new insights into grazing dynamics within estuarine and marine microbial food webs.

items.name: Yen-Po Wang
items.title: Comparing the Effects of Viral Lysis and Nanoflagellate Grazing on DOC Quantity and Bioavailability

abstract.authors: YEN-PO WANG*, FENG-HSUN CHANG
abstract.abstract:
This study investigates how nanoflagellate grazing and viral lysis influence dissolved organic carbon (DOC) quantity and bioavailability in coastal waters.
Modified dilution experiments were conducted using seawater collected from ChaoJin, Taiwan.<0.2 μm and <30 kDa seawater filtrates were used for grazing and viral dilution series, respectively. DOC measurements and subsequent dark incubations assessed changes in DOC quantity and bioavailability.
The viral dilution series generally showed higher DOC concentration-ratio and lability responses than the grazing series.
These patterns suggest that viral processes may contribute to changes in DOC quantity and bioavailability. Further microbial mortality measurements and filtration controls are needed to clarify their contribution relative to grazing.

items.name: Mao-Che Huang
items.aff: Department of Bioenvironmental Systems Engineering, National Taiwan University
items.title: Seasonal comparison of predation rate and viral lysis rate

abstract.authors: MAO-CHE HUANG
abstract.abstract: Picoplankton refers to the portion of plankton with cell sizes between 0.2 and 2 micrometers, accounting for approximately half of primary productivity on average. Picoplankton die in two ways: first, through predation, which accounts for 30% to 70% of grazing mortality; second, through viral lysis. Viral lysis can lead to mortality rates of 10% to 50%, thus it can be considered a major cause of bacterial death, and in some cases, its impact can rival that of predation-induced mortality. Therefore, this study aims to explore the seasonal proportional relationship between predation and lysis。I compared the grazing mortality rate and viral lysis rate data from March to August. The results showed that the closer the season progressed toward summer, the higher the net growth rate of heterotrophic bacteria and the higher the mortality rate, but the viral lysis rate did not change much and even showed a slight downward trend.

items.name: Yun-Hsin Lee
items.aff: Institute of Oceanography, National Taiwan University
items.title: High-Frequency Lagrangian Sampling Reveals a Delayed Population Response of Marine Group II Archaea to Environmental Perturbation

abstract.authors: LEE, YUN-HSIN
abstract.abstract: Genomic evidence suggests uncultivated Candidatus Poseidoniales (MGII archaea) rely on algal-derived organic matter, yet in situ standing stocks correlate with ambient nutrients and lag behind primary production. However, compositional biases, shifts in water masses, and the lack of direct carbon flux measurements have obscured the magnitude and timing of MGII responses to environmental change. Here, we tracked a water mass during a 7-day high-frequency Lagrangian cruise in the southern East China Sea, with sampling conducted every 6 h, and quantified MGIIa and MGIIb absolute abundances using amplicon sequencing with an internal genomic DNA spike-in. We found that absolute MGII abundance did not spatially align with peak phytoplankton biomass at the Deep Chlorophyll Maximum (DCM), contrary to the expectation that MGII archaea closely track phytoplankton biomass. Notably, a transient surface nutrient pulse observed during the time series was followed by a surge in absolute MGII standing stocks 6 hours later, capturing a discrete in situ response lag and demonstrating their capacity for rapid population expansion following transient perturbations. In summary, this suggests that MGII populations may not respond immediately after an environmental pulse but instead exhibit a multi-hour delay.

items.name: Yi-Ru Hsieh
items.title: High-frequency assessment of microbial plankton regulation and disturbance responses in an oyster-farming lagoon

abstract.authors: *Yi-Ru Hsieh, Feng-Hsun Chang, An-Yi Tsai, Cheng-Han Tsai
abstract.abstract: Microbial plankton dynamics in shallow coastal lagoons are regulated by bottom-up resource availability and top-down grazing, while their relative importance may shift rapidly under environmental variability and disturbance. We conducted a 21-day high-frequency field study in Chi-gu Lagoon, a shallow oyster-farming lagoon in southwestern Taiwan, to investigate how microbial plankton regulation varies through time and responds to episodic environmental disturbance. At a focal oyster-farming site, paired day and night sampling was conducted throughout the study, with replicated dilution experiments used to assess phytoplankton growth and grazing mortality. Additional sampling at sites with contrasting oyster-farming intensity provided a spatial comparison on selected occasions. The study period also encompassed a typhoon and heavy rainfall, enabling observations across pre-disturbance, disturbance, and recovery phases. Biological sampling was accompanied by measurements of nutrients and microbial community composition, while temperature, salinity, and turbidity were recorded continuously at one-minute intervals. This integrated design provides a framework for examining short-term variability in bottom-up and top-down regulation and how microbial food-web processes respond to environmental disturbance in a highly dynamic coastal ecosystem.

items.name: Estefania Lourdres Anak Sima
items.title: Seasonal Pattern in the Size-Trophic Position Relationship of a Subtropical Reservoir Plankton Community

abstract.authors: Estefania Lourdres Sima*, Chih-hao Hsieh, Chun-wei Chang, Pei-chi Ho
abstract.abstract: Body size is a fundamental trait that structures aquatic food webs by determining predator-prey mass ratios (PPMR). In simple, size-structured ecosystems, trophic position (TP) increases linearly with body size. However, empirical studies reveal that size-TP relationships frequently deviate from linearity, creating non-linear structure. This leads to the research questions: “What are the seasonal patterns in the size-based trophic position relationship?” and “How do environmental changes influence the size-based trophic position relationship in aquatic ecosystems?”. This study aims to investigate seasonal patterns of size-trophic position relationships of the planktonic food web across contrasting mixing regimes in subtropical Feitsui Reservoir. Carbon (δ^13 C)and nitrogen (δ^15 N) stable isotope ratios were analysed to estimate the TP of each size fraction relative to basal sources. Size-TP relationships were evaluated using linear regression. Preliminary results demonstrate that while the overall size-TP relationship was positive across the year, it was statistically significant and steepest exclusively during winter. During spring, summer and autumn, the relationship became non-significant, with points scattering away from the linear regression model. These findings suggest that seasonal hydrographic mixing may affect the linearity of energy transfer pathways in subtropical freshwater ecosystems.

items.name: Hsin-Hsin Hsiao
items.title: Influence of terrestrial inputs on the community respiration rate of FeiTsui Reservoir

abstract.authors: Hsin-Hsin Hsiao*, Chun-Wei Chang, Chao-Chen Lai
abstract.abstract: Enclosed aquatic systems are often metabolically autotrophic and act as carbon sinks, with primary production generally greater than or equal to community respiration. However, terrestrial inputs introduce allochthonous organic carbon that support microbial respiration, potentially shifting the system toward a heterotrophic state and net carbon release. Because extreme weather can alter the allochthonous inputs from terrestrial systems, its effects on the balance between carbon emissions and sequestration in aquatic systems through changes in terrestrial inputs required further evaluation. To address this issue, we combined a soil-addition experiment with in situ measurements of community respiration to assess how respiration rates respond to soil addition under different environmental conditions. Field measurements showed that respiration rates were significantly lower after extreme rainfall events than before the events at depths of 2 and 10 m (p = 0.01 and p = 0.03, respectively), whereas no significant difference was observed at 20 m. In the soil-addition experiment, respiration rates gradually increased over 48h. These findings suggest that terrestrial inputs likely affect the metabolic status of aquatic systems, especially following extreme rainfall events.

items.name: Fan-Syuan Lai
items.aff: Institute of Oceanography, National Taiwan University
items.title: Causal effects of population dynamics, prey, environment, and fishing on fish population spatial variability in the North Sea

abstract.authors: Fan- Syuan Lai*, Chih-hao Hsieh
abstract.abstract: A fish population with highly aggregated spatial distribution (i.e., high spatial variability in biomass) can have reduced population resilience and recovery potential following environmental disturbances. Although drivers influencing fish population spatial variability have been a research focus, clear causal linkages remain limited. In particular, bottom-up (i.e., abundance, composition, and spatial variation of prey) effects on spatial variability of marine predatory fishes have not been carefully examined. Using 34-year fish survey data from the North Sea, we applied empirical dynamic modeling (EDM) to quantify the effects of population dynamics (i.e., abundance and age structure of the target population), environmental factors, prey fields (i.e., total abundance, spatial variability, and taxonomic compositions of prey), and fishing on spatial variability of each target fish population. Analyzing six fish populations where data are sufficient, we found that prey beta-diversity exerted positive causal influences on predator (whiting and plaice) spatial variability, suggesting prey-selective feeding behavior shapes fish distributions as prey composition shifts in space. In contrast, high abundance or diverse age structure of fish helps reduce population spatial variability in five species. The causal impacts of temperature and climate indices varied among species in both direction and magnitude, whereas effects of annual fishing mortality were scarcely detected as a causal variable for spatial variability of the target population. Our findings underscore the importance of incorporating spatially explicit drivers into fisheries management.

items.name: You-Ci Fan
items.aff: Institute of Oceanography, National Taiwan University
items.title: Environmental Change Effects on Community Assembly of North Sea Fishes: Insights from Functional and Phylogenetic Community Structure

abstract.authors: You-Ci Fan*, Chih-hao Hsieh
abstract.abstract: Climate-related environmental change can restructure communities by driving non-random species gains and losses, thereby generating directional shifts in community structure. However, the temporal dynamics of marine fish communities and their association with environmental changes remain poorly understood. In this study, we used environmental and fish community data from the North Sea (1999 –2025) and quantified functional structure using standardized effect sizes of mean pairwise functional distance (SES.MFD) and mean nearest-neighbour functional distance (SES.MNFD), and phylogenetic structure using mean pairwise phylogenetic distance (SES.MPD) and mean nearest-taxon distance (SES.MNTD). Our results showed greater temporal environmental variability and greater changes in community structure in the southern than northern North Sea. In the south, SES.MFD increased after 2015 in Q1, SES.MPD increased in Q1 but decreased in Q3, and SES.MNTD increased after 2012 in Q1. These changes were correlated with nutrient, primary production, and salinity. In contrast, the north showed only decreasing SES.MNFD and SES.MNTD in Q3, correlated with nitrate and salinity. Overall, temporal changes of North Sea fish community were spatially and seasonally heterogeneous, with stronger changes in the more environmentally variable southern region.

items.name: Chun Fei Cheung
items.title: Larger Juveniles under Fluctuating Temperatures due to Prolonged Larval Duration: Intertidal Fish as a Case Study

abstract.authors: Chun Fei Cheung*, Hui-Yu Wang, Seiji Arakaki
abstract.abstract: Fish larval traits, like size when settling in juvenile habitat (settlement size) and time spent before settlement (pelagic larval duration, PLD), are temperature-sensitive and influence juvenile survival and dispersal. Although warming and fluctuating temperatures are known to impact fish size, impacts on larval stage remain poorly understood. We examine how temperature affects these larval traits and the possible pathway in the thermally dynamic intertidal zone. 2604 fish representing 10 species, with individual-based temperature anomaly and variability, representing whether larvae experience higher/lower and more/less fluctuation in mean daily temperature compared to species means, were sampled across Japan and Taiwan. Mixed-effects models reveal that neither temperature anomaly nor variability directly affects settlement size. However, per 1 °C² increase in temperature variability, PLD lengthens by 1.96%, and per 1% increase in PLD, settlement size increases by 0.44%, indicating an indirect pathway from temperature variability to settlement size through PLD. Species-specific PLD responses to temperature variability ranged from 0.33% to 3.49% per 1 °C² increase, and these species-specific slopes were positively correlated with median tidepool depth distribution, indicating stronger PLD responses among deeper-water-associated species. Under anticipated more fluctuating temperatures under warming, subtidal fish larvae may be particularly affected.

items.name: Shan-En Chen
items.title: Benthic Habitat Mapping via Foundation Model Representation Using A Multi-Modal Snorkeling Survey

abstract.authors: Shan-En Chen*, Wei-Chen Tung, Felipe MG Mattos, Tzu-Yi Chuang, Frederic Sinniger, Tzu-Hao Lin
abstract.abstract: Habitat mapping is essential for characterizing ecological patterns, yet ground truth annotations aren’t always available because they require time and expertise. Foundation models enable semantic representation learning to extract meaningful features for habitat mapping, yet their potential in low-visibility benthic environments remains under-explored. We collected spatial, visual, and acoustic data during a one-day snorkeling transect survey in Nakijin, Okinawa, Japan, across a substrate mosaic of sand, rock, and branching coral. A Gaussian mixture model was trained on DINOv2 representations and validated against expert annotations in a sand/branching-coral sub-area. Classification achieved a ROC-AUC score of 0.9886. Qualitative analysis of the full transect showed the representation meaningfully captured complex, multi-substrate mosaics beyond the validated sub-area. We further derived eco-acoustic indicators, including snapping shrimp intensity and fish call abundance, which could link acoustic activity to substrate type in further studies. These findings demonstrate the practical value of foundation-model representation learning for scalable benthic habitat mapping, with promising extensibility to other complex habitats. Future work will explore multi-modal integration, fusing visual and acoustic representations across multiple foundation models.

items.name: Ee Suan Tan
items.title: From Moonlight to Spawning: Regulation of GVBD in Galaxea fascicularis

abstract.authors: Ee Suan Tan, Che-hung Lin, Luigi Colin, Aziz J Mulla, Chia-Ling Fong, Felipe Mattos, Chieh-Hsuan Lee, Yuu Ishii, Yoko Nozawa, Christian R Voolstra, Shunichi Takahashi
abstract.abstract: Coral mass spawning is an annual event in which numerous colonies release gametes with precise synchrony. As most reef-building corals spawn only once a year, the timing of gamete release is critical for maximizing fertilization. Recent studies demonstrated that moonlight suppresses spawning, and that the dark period between sunset and moonrise serves as a spawning cue. However, the mechanisms underlying this regulation remain poorly understood. In this study, we investigated the effect of the dark cue on gametogenesis and gene expression in the coral Galaxea fascicularis. Coral fragments were maintained in tanks with and without cue, and samples were collected daily until spawning occurred. Histological and transcriptomic analyses were performed to examine changes in gonadal development and molecular pathways associated with the cue. Under dark condition, all colonies spawned synchronously, whereas no spawning occurred in the control under artificial moonlight. Our results show that the dark cue regulates critical stages of gametogenesis, enabling progression toward gamete maturation and spawning. Transcriptomic analysis further revealed sets of genes responsive to the cue, including both common and sex-specific patterns of regulation. Together, these findings provide new insights into the molecular and cellular basis of how environmental cues, particularly lunar cycles, regulate coral reproduction.

items.name: Fong-Huei Lin
items.title: Sunset manipulation suggests that sunset cues and an endogenous clock both contribute to reproductive timing in Dipsastraea speciosa

abstract.authors: Fong Huei Lin*, Yuki Yoshioka, Yi Jyun Luo, Che Hung Lin
abstract.abstract: Many broadcast-spawning corals release gametes within a narrow window after sunset. Spawning synchrony is essential for reproduction success, but whether this timing is determined by sunset alone or is also regulated by an endogenous clock remains unclear. We investigated how altered sunset timing affected reproductive events in the merulinid coral Dipsastraea speciosa. Here we show that advancing sunset by 2 h induced earlier germinal vesicle breakdown (GVBD), egg-sperm bundle formation, and spawning. In contrast, delaying sunset by 2 h or maintaining constant light did not alter the timing of these events, which occurred at the same clock times as in the control. Moreover, preliminary RNA-seq analysis suggested that some gene expression patterns also shifted earlier under advanced sunset. Together, these findings suggest that sunset acts as a cue for the timing of coral spawning. However, spawning did not occur later when sunset was delayed, suggesting that an endogenous clock may also regulate its timing. Further analysis of the RNA-seq data may provide molecular evidence for this possibility.

items.name: Hidemi Shimbo
items.title: Bleaching as an opportunity for corals to establish new algal partnerships

abstract.authors: Hidemi Shimbo*, Ee Suan Tan, Shunichi Takahashi
abstract.abstract:
Bleaching opens the possibility for corals to get new symbiotic partners.
Corals host algal symbionts of the family Symbiodiniaceae and rely on their photosynthesis for survival and growth. When corals are exposed to environmental stress such as rising seawater temperatures, they lose their symbionts and bleach. However, bleached corals are still alive, and some can recover if they can repopulate the algal symbionts. Previous studies have reported the changes in symbiont composition before and after bleaching, and thermotolerant symbionts have been found in corals that have recovered from bleaching. Although these observations suggest that bleaching occurs to obtain new algal symbionts suitable for changing environments, it has not been investigated yet. To examine whether bleaching enhances the acquisition of new algal symbionts, we conducted experiments using the model organism sea anemone Exaiptasia. We inoculated algal symbionts into both healthy (control) and bleached hosts, and found that bleached hosts acquired more algal symbionts than controls. Our findings suggest that the expulsion of resident symbionts promotes the uptake of new symbionts. In short, bleaching is a double-edged sword: it acts as an environmental adaptation, but it also leads to starvation.

items.name: Kenji Toyota
items.title: Morphological changes induced by parasitic crustaceans in decapod crustacean hosts

abstract.authors: Kenji Toyota*, Asami Kajimoto
abstract.abstract: Parasitic crustaceans can modify host sexual traits, but the extent to which these effects vary among host–parasite combinations remains poorly understood. Rhizocephalan barnacles and bopyrid isopods offer opportunities to examine such morphological alterations in decapod hosts. Here, we quantitatively compared morphological feminization associated with rhizocephalan parasitism in hermit crabs of the genus Pagurus. Specimens collected at multiple Japanese localities between 2018 and 2025 were classified as unparasitized females, unparasitized males, or parasitized males. We assessed the presence of female-type pleopods and measured shield and cheliped lengths to evaluate changes in secondary sexual characteristics. Parasitized males showed increased frequencies of female-type pleopods in several host–parasite combinations. Cheliped shortening was also evident in some combinations, with effect size analyses indicating that relative cheliped lengths approached those of unparasitized females. In other combinations, this convergence toward female morphology was not observed. These findings demonstrate that the morphological traits affected and the degree of feminization vary among host–parasite combinations. Comparative analyses across parasitic crustaceans and their hosts may help clarify the diversity of host phenotypic modification and provide a basis for investigating its underlying mechanisms.

items.name: Hsuan-Wien Chen
items.title: Parasite Spillover and Spillback Between Invasive African Sacred Ibises and Native Herons in Taiwan

abstract.authors: Yi-Ling Chen, Xin-Ru Lee, Cheng-Te Yao, Hsuan-Wien Chen
abstract.abstract: Parasite spillover occurs when invasive hosts transmit their parasites to native hosts, while spillback arises when invasive hosts acquire native parasites and subsequently amplify their transmission. Both processes can reshape host–parasite dynamics and affect ecosystem health. In Taiwan, the African Sacred Ibis (Threskiornis aethiopicus), a long-established invasive waterbird, has the potential to introduce non-native parasites or alter the transmission of local parasites, yet empirical evidence remains limited. This study investigated parasitic infections in African Sacred Ibises and native herons inhabiting Taiwanese coastal wetlands, using morphological and molecular approaches to assess potential spillover and spillback events. Two major helminth parasites were identified in the African Sacred Ibis populations: an acanthocephalan (Southwellina hispida) and a trematode (Patagifer sp.). Comparative analyses with parasites from native herons suggest that S. hispida, a generalist infecting multiple waterbird species, represents a likely case of spillback, whereas Patagifer sp., which exhibit host specificity, may indicate potential spillover. These findings provide new insights into parasite exchange between invasive and native waterbirds and underscore the broader ecological implications of host–parasite interactions in invasion biology.

items.name: Yun-Wei Chou
items.aff: Institute of Oceanography, National Taiwan University
items.title: Unraveling Time-Varying Environmental Effects on Mosquito Population Dynamics in Tainan, Taiwan

abstract.authors: 周昀韋*(Yun-Wei Chou*), 莊昕寰(Hsin-Huan Chuang), 蔡政翰(Cheng-Han Tsai), 周采頻(Tsai-Pin Chou), 劉凱丞(Kai-Cheng Liu), 劉鎮(Jhen Liu), 陳建河(Jen-Her Chen), 黃旌集(Chin-Gi Huang), 郭鴻基(Hung-Chi Kuo), 王偉仲(Wei-Chung Wang), 蔡孟裕(Meng-Yu Tsai), 謝志豪(Chih-hao Hsieh)
abstract.abstract: Mosquito–environment dynamics are often nonlinear, with the direction and strength of environmental effects varying with system state. Linear models with fixed parameters may inadequately capture these relationships, limiting our understanding of population fluctuations. We integrated weekly ovitrap egg counts and meteorological data from Tainan, Taiwan, within 2 km hexagonal grids. MDR S-map models were fitted separately to each grid to estimate time-varying coefficients for environmental variables at different time lags. Relationships between mean coefficients and urbanization intensity were also examined across grids. Current-week temperature, precipitation lagged by two weeks, and relative humidity lagged by two weeks showed positive associations with egg counts, whereas precipitation lagged by one week and wind speed showed negative associations. With increasing urbanization, the coefficients for precipitation lagged by one week tended to become more negative, while those for precipitation lagged by two weeks tended to become more positive. These patterns suggest that urbanization may be associated with differences in mosquito responses to precipitation. By examining time-varying coefficients, this study characterizes mosquito–environment relationships across temporal lags and land-use contexts, contributing to a dynamical understanding of mosquito population fluctuations and informing mosquito monitoring and control.

items.name: Hsin-Huan Chuang
items.aff: Institute of Oceanography, National Taiwan University
items.title: Predicting Nonlinear Dynamics of Mosquito Populations in Tainan with Environmental Data

abstract.authors: 莊昕寰(Hsin-Huan Chuang)*, 周昀韋(Yun-Wei Chou), 蔡政翰(Cheng-Han Tsai), 周采頻(Tsai-Pin Chou), 劉凱丞(Kai-Cheng Liu), 劉鎮(Jhen Liu), 陳建河(Jen-Her Chen), 黃旌集(Chin-Gi Huang), 郭鴻基(Hung-Chi Kuo), 王偉仲(Wei-Chung Wang), 蔡孟裕(Meng-Yu Tsai), 謝志豪(Chih-hao Hsieh)
abstract.abstract: Mosquito populations respond to environmental conditions through complex nonlinear relationships that are difficult to characterize using conventional linear approaches. This study applies Empirical Dynamic Modeling (EDM) to predict mosquito activity in Tainan, Taiwan. Weekly ovitrap egg counts and meteorological data were integrated into grid-based time series for analysis. We applied Sequential Locally Weighted Global Linear Maps (S-Map) and Gaussian Process Empirical Dynamic Modeling (GPEDM) to evaluate predictive performance and uncertainty. S-Map achieved a mean correlation of 0.770 between predictions and observations across the study grids, capturing variation in mosquito activity. GPEDM achieved a mean correlation of 0.640, with predictive intervals containing 92.23% of observations with valid predictions. These findings demonstrate the potential of nonlinear dynamical methods for mosquito prediction. Combining predictive estimates with uncertainty information may inform mosquito surveillance planning and vector management.

items.name: Jhen Liu
items.title: Indirect effects of deforestation and elevation shape abundance of Aedes albopictus through temperature, water turbidity, and invertebrate natural enemies

abstract.authors: Jhen Liu*, Jia-Yi Li, Kun-Hsien Tsai, Chi-Chien Kuo
abstract.abstract: Population abundance of Aedes albopictus is an important indicator of the potential risk of mosquito-borne diseases, but its distribution and abundance may vary among habitat types and elevations because of differences in local environmental conditions. To better understand the ecological mechanisms underlying variation in mosquito abundance, we conducted a systematic survey across different habitat types and elevations and evaluated the hypothesized direct and indirect relationships among environmental variables. We surveyed mosquitoes, potential mosquito predators, and water quality across three habitat types and three elevations in northern Taiwan. Mosquitoes were sampled monthly for one year using three sampling methods. A total of 4,667 Ae. albopictus individuals were collected, and 238 potential mosquito predators were recorded. Ae. albopictus was consistently more abundant in anthropogenic habitats across all three elevations. Furthermore, elevation and habitat type were associated with local temperature and water turbidity, which were in turn related to mosquito abundance and the occurrence of potential predators. Our results demonstrate that habitat characteristics can influence Ae. albopictus populations through both direct and indirect ecological pathways, highlighting the importance of considering local environmental context when assessing spatial variation in mosquito abundance.

items.name: Jo-Hsun Chiu
items.aff: Institute of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, National Taiwan University
items.title: Human-dominated landscapes support high diversity of wintering birds

abstract.authors: Jo-Hsun Chiu*, Da-Li Lin
abstract.abstract: Human-dominated landscapes, including agricultural and aquaculture landscapes, are often considered to have limited value for wildlife conservation. However, growing evidence suggests that these landscapes can support biodiversity and provide important ecosystem functions. Their role in conserving migratory species remains poorly understood. Using data from the Taiwan New Year Bird Count, we examined associations between wintering bird diversity and land-use types across different regions of Taiwan. Generalized linear mixed models revealed that northern and southwestern Taiwan supported higher wintering bird richness, with aquaculture landscapes exhibiting particularly high diversity. Agricultural landscapes were positively associated with the occurrence of 4 wintering waterbird species, 6 landbird species, and 1 raptor species, while aquaculture landscapes, particularly in southwestern Taiwan, were associated with 13 wintering waterbird species. These findings demonstrate that human-dominated production landscapes can provide valuable habitats for migratory birds and different production landscapes can support distinct assemblages of species. As natural habitats continue to decline worldwide, promoting biodiversity-friendly management of agricultural and aquaculture landscapes could help compensate for habitat loss and enhance the conservation of migratory birds.

items.name: Yu-Zhi Zhang
items.aff: Hydrotech Research Institute, National Taiwan University
items.title: Temporal Partitioning and Co-existence Strategies of Medium-to-Large Mammals across Natural and Plantation Forests

abstract.authors: Zhang,Yu-Zhi*, Huang,Jing-Lun
abstract.abstract:
This study investigated the impacts of forest monoculture on the temporal co-existence mechanisms of medium-to-large mammalian communities. Camera trap monitoring was conducted during the autumn and winter seasons of 2025–2026 across three natural forest sites and one plantation forest site. Species relative abundance was evaluated using the Occurrence Index (OI). Daily activity rhythms were quantified via Kernel Density Estimation, and temporal co-existence strategies were analyzed using the overlap coefficient. Our results indicated that the Formosan reeve's muntjac ( Muntiacus reevesi micrurus ) maintained an absolute numerical dominance across all habitat types. However, spatial community analysis revealed severe behavioral restriction and localized clustering within the plantation forest, driving a significant increase in the spatial turnover rate (~0.55) during winter. Regarding temporal partitioning, species-pair overlap analysis demonstrated that sympatric herbivores and carnivores effectively achieved coexistence through microhabitat selection in natural forests. Conversely, within the structurally simplified and resource-limited plantation forest, several species exhibited significant temporal phase shifts, modifying their typical diurnal or crepuscular rhythms to achieve temporal avoidance. This study quantifies how plantation monocultures alter the spatio-temporal utilization strategies of mammalian communities. These findings provide critical baseline data for future ecological restoration and habitat management of plantation forests.
Keywords: Camera trapping, Forest monoculture, Activity rhythm, Temporal overlap, Muntiacus reevesi micrurus

items.name: Wei-Chien Tsai
items.aff: Department of Life Science, National Taiwan Normal University
items.title: Comparison of Population Structure and Morphology of the Yellow Pond Turtle (Mauremys mutica) between Urban Farmland and a Forest Aquatic Pond

abstract.authors:
Wei-Chien Tsai<sup>1*</sup>, Yuan-Cheng Cheng<sup>1</sup>, Chun-Wen Chang<sup>2</sup>, Si-Min Lin<sup>1</sup>
<sup>1</sup> Department of Life Science, National Taiwan Normal University
<sup>2</sup> Fushan Research Center, Taiwan Forestry Research Institute
abstract.abstract: The yellow pond turtle (Mauremys mutica), a species native to Taiwan, is listed as Endangered (EN) by the IUCN and is designated as an Endangered Species of Protected Wildlife in Taiwan. Beyond protected, low-disturbance habitats, little is known about whether agricultural wetlands on the urban fringe can support the persistence of its populations. In this study, we compared two sites with sharply contrasting levels of anthropogenic disturbance. Urban farmland in Shulin District, New Taipei City, represents a highly disturbed site, where high densities of the invasive red-eared slider (Trachemys scripta elegans) co-occur with the native Chinese stripe-necked turtle (Mauremys sinensis), which poses a risk of hybridization. In contrast, the aquatic pond at Fushan Botanical Garden, Yilan, represents a low-disturbance site that is free of invasive species and provides a complete habitat meeting the needs of the species’ entire life history. Turtles were live-captured using cylindrical fish traps and individually marked by marginal scute notching. A total of 98 individuals were recorded (47 at Shulin and 51 at Fushan). Six morphological traits were measured, body condition was assessed using the residuals of a linear regression of body mass on straight carapace length, and monthly variation in captures was expressed as catch per unit effort (CPUE). Population structure differed significantly between the two sites: the Shulin site had a higher proportion of juveniles (30/47), and its adults were predominantly female (14 females, 3 males), whereas the Fushan site was significantly dominated by adults (42/51) and had a higher proportion of males (30 males, 12 females). Morphologically, males showed no significant differences in any trait between the two sites. Females at Fushan were significantly larger only in shell height; however, Shulin females exhibited significantly greater individual variation in five morphological traits, including carapace and plastron measurements, as well as in body mass. Body condition of adults did not differ significantly between the two sites, although Fushan females showed significantly greater individual variation. Captures at both sites peaked in spring and summer and dropped to their lowest levels in autumn and winter, indicating seasonality in capture rates. Our current results suggest that urban farmland may have the potential to support local reproduction and maintain a stable population of M. mutica, as the interconnected network of irrigation ditches may simultaneously provide corridors for dispersal, refuges for juveniles, and alternative food sources. In addition, we speculate that the significant difference in sex ratio between the two sites may be related to the influence of environmental temperature on sex determination; however, the exact mechanism requires confirmation with more comprehensive microhabitat temperature and population data in the future. We recommend that future conservation strategies encourage the incorporation of wildlife-friendly agricultural landscapes into ecological networks in lowland hills and urban fringes as other effective area-based conservation measures (OECMs), and the establishment of urban blue-green infrastructure, so as to create favorable habitats for the yellow pond turtle. Keywords: yellow pond turtle; population structure; morphological comparison; urban blue-green infrastructure

items.name: Sheng-Hung Lin
items.title: Improving bearing angle estimation of sika deer (Cervus nippon taiouanus) vocalizations in complex soundscapes

abstract.authors: Sheng-Hung Lin*, Shih-Ching Yen, Tzu-Hao Lin
abstract.abstract: Sound source localization is an emerging technique in ecoacoustics for investigating population dynamics and individual movement tracking. This approach relies on bearing angle estimation of sound sources. However, noise interference severely affects the robustness of estimation, particularly in complex soundscapes such as tropical forests characterized by abundant ambient noise. To address this issue, we propose using source separation to reduce noise interference and thereby enhance the robustness of spatial localization across multiple channels. In this study, we computed the time difference of arrival (TDOA) of acoustic events from multi-channel recordings of a sika deer (Cervus nippon taiouanus) population in an uplifted coral reef nature reserve, where insect sounds served as intense biophonic noise affecting TDOA estimation of the target signal. Two denoising treatments were compared: the Butterworth filter as a traditional method, and the source separation method provided by soundscape_IR. Results showed that TDOA estimation under source separation produced more continuous and convergent spatiotemporal distributions. Compared with the bandpass filter treatment, source separation achieved higher confidence levels under high-intensity noise interference. In some cases, individuals from different bearing angles could be distinguished from mixed acoustic events following TDOA enhancement. Our results support that source separation can effectively improve TDOA estimation by isolating target signals from noisy conditions, with potential applications in estimating abundance and characterizing individual and population-level behavioral dynamics in complex soundscapes.

items.name: Chuan-Kai Hsieh
items.aff: Department of Soil and Water Conservation, National Chung Hsing University
items.title: Aligning remote sensing and field survey in watershed health assessment: a case study in Central Taiwan

abstract.authors: Chuan-Kai Hsieh*, Ting-Yan Liu, Su-Chin Chen
abstract.abstract: Headwater watersheds in Taiwan are rarely assessed for ecosystem function because they lack discharge gauges, continuous water-quality monitoring and standardized biological inventories. Stream corridors, the lotic and riparian habitats where land-use decisions have the greatest marginal effect, are the least documented. We tested whether indicators derived from secondary data can complement field observation in the Zhongguakeng Creek watershed, Nantou, central Taiwan. From orthophotos spanning six decades we reconstructed a chronology of channel and riparian morphology at 130 transects spaced 100 m along the order ≥3 stream network, and derived composite indicators of four riparian functions: flood and debris attenuation, water-quality buffering, habitat connectivity and bank stabilization. In 2025–2026 we surveyed benthic macroinvertebrates and riparian vegetation across three sites and compared the field metrics with the remotely sensed indicators at reach and sub-basin scales. The orthophoto-derived indicators are compared with the field-surveyed riparian condition and biotic integrity, and the historical chronology provides rich context of fluvial and landscape morphological change. Aligning the two sources yields a transect-resolution, watershed-wide assessment that is repeatable from archival imagery and anchored by field evidence, offering a low-cost basis for prioritizing riparian management in data-scarce watersheds.

items.name: Po-Wei Huang
items.aff: Department of Life Science, National Taiwan Normal University
items.title: Container size, behavioral responses, and welfare of corn snakes (Pantherophis guttatus) under transport-related conditions

abstract.authors: Po-Wei Huang*, Yuan-Cheng Cheng, Si-Min Lin
abstract.abstract: Snakes are commonly kept in small, transparent, unenriched containers during display, sale, and transport, raising concerns about restricted behavior and welfare. We examined how container size affects behavioral responses of corn snakes (Pantherophis guttatus) under static, simulated vibration, and real vehicle transport conditions. Ten juvenile corn snakes were individually tested in three container sizes (small: 14.5 × 11 × 7.5 cm; medium: 30 × 20 × 15 cm; large: 40 × 30 × 20 cm), with at least 48 h between trials. The first 60 min of each condition were analyzed for stationary and resting behavior. Under static and vehicle conditions, stationary and resting durations were significantly longer in the small container than in the medium and large containers. Under simulated vibration, both durations differed significantly among all three sizes, with the longest durations in the small container and the shortest in the medium container. These findings suggest that smaller containers may facilitate sustained resting and provide greater physical stability during short-term transport, although responses may depend on the pattern and direction of movement.

items.name: Janus Olajuan Boediman
items.title: Camouflage strategies in moss and lichen morphs of Trachyzulpha formosana (Orthoptera: Tettigoniidae)

abstract.authors: Janus Olajuan Boediman*, Lung-Chun Huang, Sheng-Shan Lu, Hsin-Chieh Tang, Chen-Pan Liao, Hui-Yun Tseng
abstract.abstract: Many organisms use camouflage to avoid predation. Background matching is a camouflage strategy in which the organism hides on backgrounds that resemble their appearance. Other strategies do not require exact background matching, such as masquerade or disruptive coloration. In this study, we investigated the camouflage strategies of a Taiwan-endemic katydid, Trachyzulpha formosana, which exhibits two distinct morphs: one resembling moss and one resembling lichen. We hypothesize that each morph prefers backgrounds that match its own appearance. We evaluated their background preferences using two types of choice experiments: one with images of moss and lichen, and one with real moss and lichen attached to the images. We also applied visual modeling to determine whether predators can distinguish katydids from their backgrounds. In both experiments, moss-morph katydids showed a preference for moss background. Lichen-morph katydids also showed a preference for moss, but only in the experiment with real substrate. Visual modeling suggests that predators can distinguish both katydid morphs from non-matching backgrounds, but not from matching backgrounds. Our results reveal a mismatch between appearance and substrate choice. Only the moss morph selected its matching background, suggesting that the lichen morph may rely on other camouflage mechanisms.

items.name: Jing-Lun Huang
items.aff: Hydrotech Research Institute, National Taiwan University
items.title: The utility of nestedness structure for predicting species richness

abstract.authors: Jing-Lun Huang*
abstract.abstract: Species accumulation curves (SACs) are essential macroecological tools for estimating regional species richness, yet their accuracy is constrained by data input order and the subjective choice of extrapolation functions. While standard randomization methods minimize ordering bias, they often obscure vital ecological structures that contain valuable predictive information. This study is a new attempt to incorporate nested community structures to enhance the predictive power of SAC fitting methods, using comprehensive Taiwanese avian dataset as a prime example. We evaluated the degree to which ordering data based on nested structures—rather than randomized inputs—improves total species richness estimates. These data-ordering methods were fitted to negative exponential, logarithmic, and Clench functions at multiple spatial scales, including national level and 10x10 km grid cells. Ordering data based on nestedness is expected to detectably increase the predictability of species richness at finer spatial scales, especially coupled with the logarithmic function, due to a perfect complementary effect between community structure and mathematical model. This study aims to demonstrate that leveraging non-random ecosystem heterogeneity, such as nestedness, transforms subjective empirical choices of prediction curves into an objective, data-driven framework to optimize sampling efforts and accurately assess biodiversity in complex, species-rich island landscapes.
abstract.affiliation: Hydrotech Research Institute, National Taiwan University

items.name: Song-Yang Tu
items.title: A Study on the Choice of Response Variables in Diversity Research

abstract.authors: Song-Yang Tu; Chun-Huo Chiu
abstract.abstract: The species composition of communities in ecosystem can be influenced by environmental or climatic factors. Biodiversity may also change due to the impact of global warming. To understand the relationship between species diversity and climatic factors, researchers often use species diversity analysis to construct statistical model between climatic factors and species richness estimates, aiming to explore the relationship between variables, and to evaluate model performance. However, the suitability of using estimated species richness as the response variable in diversity analysis has rarely been systematically discussed in previous studies. The methods for estimating species richness as response variables are evaluated and compared based on regression coefficient estimates, test statistics, and the significance rate of explanatory variables. The simulation results show that, for regression coefficient  estimation, under the condition of minimizing bias, the parametric species richness estimators, Gamma-Poisson-based (𝐺𝑃), is considered more suitable as response variables for species richness diversity analysis in abundance data. For model test statistics, the standardized species richness estimation method based on sample coverage, yields test statistics closer to the true model, making it more suitable as a proxy for the test statistics of number of species in communities.

items.name: Cong Zhou
items.title: How rapid evolution of mutualism affects the coexistence of competing species

abstract.authors: Cong Zhou*, Masato Yamamichi
abstract.abstract: Understanding how competing species coexist despite the competitive exclusion principle has long been a central question in ecology. Recent studies have highlighted two factors that strongly influence competition and coexistence: mutualistic interactions and rapid evolution. However, how these two factors jointly shape competitive dynamics remains unclear. Using a three-species Lotka–Volterra model with two competitors and one mutualist, we show that rapid evolution of the mutualist can drastically alter coexistence outcomes. We model the evolution of two mutualistic traits: total mutualistic investment and partner preference. Evolutionary changes in these traits generally reduce niche differences within the framework of modern coexistence theory, thereby shrinking the parameter space that permits coexistence and promoting either competitive exclusion or priority effects, whereby early-arriving species monopolize niches. Consequently, models that ignore evolutionary dynamics may substantially overestimate the potential for coexistence. Our results demonstrate that the effects of mutualism on species coexistence are evolutionarily dynamic and underscore the importance of incorporating rapid evolution of species interactions into modern coexistence theory.

items.name: Hsiang-Chih Lo
items.aff: Institute of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, National Taiwan University
items.title: How to conduct invasion analysis for structured populations? Analytical insights and numerical recipes

abstract.authors: Joe Wan, Hsiang-Chih Lo*, Guan-Yu Chen, Shiang-Chi Huang, Jia-Zhen Liu, Chin-Te Tsai, Po-Ju Ke
abstract.abstract: A species’ growth rate when rare, known as its invasion growth rate, helps ecologists understand species persistence and coexistence. However, estimating this rate becomes challenging when individuals differ in their life stages or other states. For example, a stage-structured population introduced as juveniles may initially decline, while the same species introduced as adults may increase, making initial growth an unreliable indicator of long-term invasion success. We developed a unified framework for distinguishing these transient responses from long-term population growth while the invader remains too rare to alter its environment. Using a stage-structured competition model as an example, we showed that populations with different initial stage compositions converge to the same invasion growth rate once transient differences in stage composition disappear. With this insight, we demonstrated how analytical expressions of the invasion growth rate can be derived using timescale separation and matrix theory. Mathematical calculations and computer simulations yield consistent estimates in our worked example. We further applied the framework to models of intraguild predation, plant–soil feedback, and parasitoid interactions, illustrating how invasion growth can be quantified in structured population models when individuals differ in developmental stage, soil environment, or infection status.
abstract.affiliation: Institute of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, National Taiwan University

items.name: Yi-De Lee
items.aff: Department of Physics, National Central University
items.title: A pollinator crisis can decrease plant abundance despite pollinators being herbivores at the larval stage

abstract.authors: Yi-De Lee*, Tomoyuki Yokoi, Takefumi Nakazawa
abstract.abstract: Pollinating insects are decreasing worldwide due to various environmental stresses (so-called pollinator crisis), raising concerns that plant productivity could be undermined in natural and agricultural ecosystems. To date, however, few studies have reported a concurrent decline in both pollinators and plants, and little is known about when a “plant crisis” occurs. Here, we propose that anthropogenic environmental stresses on pollinating insects (e.g. climate change, habitat loss, and pesticide usage) can negatively affect herbivorous insects (e.g., pollinator larvae and crop pests) as well, and effects of pollinator declines may be masked by positive effects of herbivore declines. To test the idea, we theoretically investigated plant population dynamics mediated by two insect groups: one representing a pollinator that is mutualistic at the adult stage but antagonistic at the larval stage, and the other representing a non-structured pest herbivore. Our model revealed that environmental stresses (increasing insect mortality) can have counterintuitive effects on plants. Nonetheless, plant abundance generally decreases with decreasing pollinator abundance, especially when plant populations grow slowly without pollinators, when pollinators are effective mutualists, or when pollinators are susceptible to environmental stresses. These findings offer a theoretical basis for assessing the pollinator crisis for biodiversity conservation and agricultural management.
abstract.affiliation: Department of Physics, National Central University

items.name: Gaku Takimoto
items.title: Mesopredator release from carcass provisioning apex predators

abstract.authors: Gaku Takimoto*, Hana Suenaga
abstract.abstract: Predators play diverse and crucial roles in determining the structure and dynamics of ecological communities. Human activities, such as overexploitation and habitat destruction, drive the decline and extinction of apex predators. The decline of apex predators often triggers mesopredator release (the population surge of mid-ranking predators). Consequently, shared prey populations can decline even further than before the apex predator's loss. This phenomenon, known as the mesopredator release effect, poses a significant challenge for biodiversity conservation involving predator management. However, the impact of losing apex predators extends beyond merely reducing direct predation on mesopredators. Mesopredators frequently scavenge carrion left by apex predators; thus, the loss of these carrion providers can negatively affect them. Conversely, scavenging often increases the mesopredator's risk of direct predation by the very apex predator providing the meal. Therefore, this provisioned carrion acts as a "fatal attraction" for mesopredators. In this presentation, we use a mathematical model to theoretically analyze how carrion provisioning and its fatal attraction influence the dynamics of mesopredator release and its subsequent effects on shared prey populations.

items.name: Aoi Sato
items.title: Toward the Theory of Death-feigning

abstract.authors: Aoi Sato*, Atsushi Yamauchi
abstract.abstract:
Death-feigning is an anti-predator trait in which prey remains motionless to distract predator. It is known that the duration time of death-feigning is often consistent within an individual but varies among individuals within a population. It is also known that duration evolves to become longer in the presence of predators. From them, we can gain two questions. Firstly, why is there a variation among population? Secondly, how the population dynamics of preys and predators and the evolutionary dynamics of duration time interact? To solve them, two models have been developed.
To solve the first problem, I made a hypothesis. That is “Prey survives by death-feigning making someone moving decoy”. By using the framework called “War of attrition game”, I verified the hypothesis. Consequently, it turned out that there was no single optimal duration time and the exponential distribution was a stable distribution within the population.
Eco-evolutionary dynamics was used to solve the second problem. Analyzing this system, it turned out that the evolution of prey could affect the maintenance of predators’ population.
This study can explain how the variation of defensive traits is made and how the evolution of it affects the population dynamics.

items.name: Haruto Tomizuka
items.title: Eco-evolutionary consequence of Batesian mimicry: imperfect mimicry & dimorphisms

abstract.authors: *Haruto Tomizuka, Yuuya Tachiki
abstract.abstract:
Batesian mimicry allows palatable prey (mimics) to avoid predation by resembling unpalatable prey (models). Natural selection is therefore expected to increase mimetic accuracy. However, the accuracy of Batesian mimicry varies widely, from perfect to imperfect resemblance, and some species exhibit dimorphisms between mimetic and non-mimetic phenotypes within a population. To identify the ecological conditions generating such diversity of Batesian mimicry, we constructed and analyzed eco-evolutionary dynamics of Batesian mimicry (Tomizuka & Tachiki 2026 Am. Nat.). Predator discrimination under uncertainty about prey palatability was modeled using signal detection theory. We assumed that acquiring mimetic traits was associated with a physiological cost, creating a trait space with two adaptive peaks corresponding to mimetic and non-mimetic phenotypes. We found that the carrying capacity of models was the primary determinant of evolutionary outcomes. 
As the carrying capacity of models increased, the evolutionary outcome shifted sequentially from non-mimicry to dimorphism, perfect mimicry, and imperfect mimicry. Dimorphism evolved when the carrying capacity of mimics slightly exceeded that of models, with evolutionary branching allowing stable coexistence of mimetic and non-mimetic phenotypes. Our results reveal that distinct states of Batesian mimicry can emerge from a single eco-evolutionary framework that links predator decision-making, population dynamics, and phenotypic evolution.

items.name: Jia-Zhen Liu
items.title: Ontogenetic shifts in plant conditioning drive species coexistence through plant-soil feedback

abstract.authors: Jia-Zhen Liu*, Ming-Chi Hsieh, Chen-Yu Lee, Joe Wan, Po-Ju Ke
abstract.abstract: Soil microbial effects from plant conditioning are key drivers of plant community competitive dynamics, and negative microbial effects are known to promote plant coexistence. However, previous studies have rarely considered the conditioning duration, despite evidence that plant–soil feedback strength may vary across ontogenetic stages. We conducted a greenhouse experiment using Bidens pilosa and Youngia japonica, where we let the two species condition the soil until either the pre-flowering or post-flowering stage. Seeds of the two species were then sown in soils with different conditioning histories. During germination, negative microbial effects were consistently weaker in soil from the pre-flowering stage than from the post-flowering stage. However, during the growth phase, microbial effects were strongly negative in soil from the pre-flowering stage, while those of the post-flowering stage shifted towards positive. In addition, we used a patch occupancy model to examine how stage-dependent microbial effects drive community dynamics. We found that seedling-conditioned negative microbial effects determine whether plant populations can persist in the system, while adult-conditioned microbial effects further regulate the size of the parameter space allowing plant coexistence. Overall, our empirical and theoretical results show that conditioning duration linked to ontogeny plays an essential role in plant community dynamics.

items.name: Tzu-Hsin Ku
items.title: Gene Flow vs. Environmental Filtering: Genomic Drivers of Bradyrhizobium Population Structure in the Native Legume Grona

abstract.authors: Tzu-Hsin Ku*, Hilary Szu Yin Shiue, Chang-Yu Chang
abstract.abstract: A microbial population's spatial scale fundamentally depends on its dispersal capacity. Because bacteria rely heavily on passive transport via environmental vectors (e.g., wind and water) or macroorganisms, we hypothesize that dispersal limitation inherently drives genetic divergence among Bradyrhizobium lineages across different spatial contexts. This limitation potentially shapes distinct genomic features even within the same plant host genus, Grona, a native Taiwanese legume. However, environmental filtering, such as soil chemical composition, can disrupt this expected pattern. Resolving the antagonistic forces between local selection and gene flow in microorganisms remains an important yet unsolved evolutionary challenge. To address this, we apply a reverse ecology approach by isolating symbiotic Bradyrhizobium strains from diverse geographic locations for whole-genome sequencing. Following de novo genome assembly, we will define the accessory genomes characterizing each bacterial population. Furthermore, genetic neutral sites will be aligned and analyzed to determine whether a distinct pattern of isolation by distance exists across the sampled regions. By elucidating these underlying genetic units within this non-model legume-rhizobia system, we aim to robustly redefine rhizobial population structures and rigorously evaluate the true ecological drivers shaping their symbiotic diversity.

items.name: I-Chih Sha
items.aff: Institute of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, National Taiwan University
items.title: Bird’s nest fern (Asplenium nidus) as a model system for studying soil microarthropod community succession

abstract.authors: I-Chih Sha*, Yu-Pei Tseng, Po-Ju Ke, Chih-Han Chang
abstract.abstract: Bird’s nest fern (Asplenium nidus) is a common tropical and subtropical epiphyte whose bowl-shaped base provides habitat for microarthropods. We investigated microarthropod community succession within bird’s nest ferns, isolating community changes from those associated with vegetation turnover.  From a Cryptomeria japonica plantation in northern Taiwan, we sampled 9 small and 9 large fern individuals to represent relatively early and late successional stages of microarthropod communities. Our findings indicated that species addition, rather than turnover, was the major process driving microarthropod community succession. Species composition and community dispersion differed significantly between small and large ferns, with large ferns exhibiting a significantly lower community dispersion and thus community convergence during succession. Oribatida and Collembola were the first and second most abundant taxa regardless of fern size. However, the relative abundance of Oribatida decreased from small to large ferns, while that of Collembola increased. This shift may reflect greater tolerance of Oribatida to the harsh environment during early succession and the addition of Oribatida predators during late succession. Together, our results highlight bird’s nest fern as a useful model system for studying microarthropod succession.
