items.name: Ching-Ning Yeh
items.title: Changes in bryophyte community composition and functional traits along a fog frequency gradient in Taiwan

abstract.authors: Ching-Ning Yeh, Boon-Chuan Ho and David Zelený
abstract.abstract: Bryophytes are non-vascular plants, sensitive to environmental conditions, and prefer to grow in humid conditions. The mountain cloud forest provides a cooler, humid environment suitable for bryophytes to occupy different habitats. Although bryophytes can persist in different habitats, the microclimate conditions might be different across habitats and fog-frequency gradients, and interact with the substrate type and bryophyte community. We want to figure out the interaction between fog and bryophyte community composition and measure functional traits to understand bryophyte persistence strategies across habitats. We collected species composition and environmental data along a horizontal transect in Northern Taiwan, with 81 microplots established across three microhabitats (tree trunks, soil, and decade wood). The environmental data show a distinct pattern along the fog frequency gradient, and the three habitats have different patterns. The mixed-effects model shows that fog and microhabitat interact with bryophyte richness, and the PCA shows that bryophyte species composition clusters by microhabitat, suggesting that community composition changes across microhabitat types.

items.name: Tomonori Kume
items.title: Does moso bamboo expansion alter evapotranspiration? A model-based comparison with conifer plantations

abstract.authors: Tomonori Kume
abstract.abstract: Moso bamboo expansion may alter forest water cycling, but its effects on evapotranspiration remain uncertain. We measured sap flux at four bamboo stands in Japan and Taiwan and developed a canopy conductance model to compare water use between bamboo forests and conifer plantations. Annual stand transpiration ranged from 460 to 560 mm, with seasonal variation largely corresponding to vapor pressure deficit. A common model incorporating responses to vapor pressure deficit, solar radiation, and temperature reproduced transpiration at the three Japanese sites but underestimated it at the Taiwanese site, suggesting additional influences such as culm age structure. We then combined modeled transpiration with published estimates of rainfall interception to compare evapotranspiration between bamboo forests and conifer plantations under standardized meteorological conditions. The comparison suggested that differences depended on stand density: bamboo forests could have higher evapotranspiration than sparse conifer plantations but lower evapotranspiration than dense plantations. These findings suggest that the hydrological consequences of bamboo expansion depend on the structure of the vegetation being replaced and highlight the need to consider stand characteristics when assessing changes in forest water use.

items.name: Miyu Kusunoki
items.title: Diversity of floral traits and fruit morphology in Cucurbitaceae plants distributed throughout the Japanese archipelago

abstract.authors: Miyu Kusunoki*, Yuki Mitsui
abstract.abstract:
The Cucurbitaceae family comprises approximately 90 genera and 950 species, most insect-pollinated and monoecious or dioecious. Floral traits vary widely in shape, size, color, and odor. Fruits are typically fleshy, varying widely in size and shape. Floral display attracts pollinators, and increased pollination frequency and pollen load promote fruit enlargement and seed production. We hypothesized that there’s a correlation between the traits in fruits and pollinator-attracting floral traits in cucurbits. In this study, using 10 species and 1 variety of wild Cucurbitaceae plants distributed across the subtropical, warm-temperate, and temperate zones of the Japanese archipelago, we analyzed floral traits associated with fruit size and seed production.
 Results show significant interspecific variation in floral morphological traits related to pollinator attraction, such as flower display size and petal length (PC1: 64.7%), and in pollen grain size and number. Seed numbers per fruit ranged from a maximum of 108.6 ± 24.9 (Trichosanthes multiloba) to a minimum of 1.3 ± 1.2 (Schizopepon bryoniifolius). Although significant variation in fruit size was observed among species (PC1: 85.2%), it showed no strong correlation with seed number. This presentation reports whether floral traits related to pollinator attraction explain interspecific variation in seed production.

items.name: Misaki Nakajima
items.aff: Laboratory of Horticultural Plant Science, Major in Agricultural Science, Graduate School of Agriculture, Kindai University
items.title: Comparison of Non-destructive Environmental DNA Sampling Methods for Analyzing Biological Communities on Woody Plants

abstract.authors: *Misaki NAKAJIMA, Akio KASHIMURA, Kinuyo YONEYA, Takeshi MIKI
abstract.abstract: Non-destructive environmental DNA (eDNA) sampling methods have recently gained attention for surveying biological communities on woody plants. Although several non-destructive eDNA sampling methods have been developed, few studies have compared the biological communities detected by different methods on the same plants. Here, we compared two non-destructive eDNA sampling methods, wipe sampling and stemflow collection, on woody plants. Biological communities detected by each method were analyzed using DNA metabarcoding to evaluate the applicability of these methods to community monitoring. We primarily focused on arthropod communities, while fungi, mammals, and birds were also targeted. eDNA samples were collected from three Quercus serrata trees from April to August 2021 in a satoyama area of the Faculty of Agriculture, Kindai University, Nara, Japan. Arthropod DNA was detected using both eDNA sampling methods. A total of 12 arthropod species were identified by wipe sampling and 18 species by stemflow collection. Trombidiformes, Hemiptera, and Lepidoptera had high read numbers in the wipe samples, whereas Lepidoptera and Symphypleona had high read numbers in the stemflow samples. Fungal eDNA is currently being analyzed, and the results for fungi and other taxonomic groups will also be presented at the conference.

items.name: Satoru Nakamura
items.aff: Entomological Laboratory, Major in Agricultural Science, Graduate School of Agriculture, Kindai University
items.title: Temporal dynamics of volatile composition in aphid-infested and neighboring komatsuna plants

abstract.authors: Satoru Nakamura*, Sota Nagano, Kinuyo Yoneya
abstract.abstract: When plants are attacked by herbivores, they release volatile compounds known as herbivore-induced plant volatiles (HIPVs). The composition and emission patterns of HIPVs vary depending on herbivore species, density, and time since the onset of herbivory. Exposure to HIPVs can also alter volatile emissions from neighboring undamaged plants. This study aimed to characterize temporal changes in volatile emissions from komatsuna (Japanese mustard spinach), Brassica rapa var. perviridis, during infestation by the green peach aphid, Myzus persicae (Sulzer), and to examine their relationship with aphid abundance. We also examined temporal changes in volatile emissions from adjacent plants without experimental aphid introduction. Under greenhouse conditions, M. persicae was introduced onto komatsuna plants, and aphid abundance and plant volatiles were monitored for approximately one month. Plant volatiles were collected three times per week from aphid-introduced plants, adjacent plants without experimental aphid introduction, and aphid-free plants protected with insect-proof mesh. Samples were analyzed by gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC–MS), and detected peaks were tentatively identified using an MS database. Principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) was used to examine temporal patterns in volatile profiles among treatments based on peak-area data.

items.name: Polina Pilieva
items.title: The role of pheromones in regulating the behavior and social structure of fire ants

abstract.authors: Polina Pilieva, John Wang
abstract.abstract:
The fire ant Solenopsis invicta provides a powerful model to study the genetic basis of social behavior. Its colony structure—having a single-queen (monogyne) or multiple-queens (polygyne)—is determined by a “social supergene’’. This supergene contains hundreds of genes, including those for odorant-binding proteins (OBPs) like Gp-9 and enzymes for cuticular hydrocarbon (CHC) synthesis, which are hypothesized to control queen recognition. This project aims to functionally validate this model by using novel CRISPR-Cas9 delivery methods (ReMOT Control, DIPA-CRISPR, Vitellotag) to enable high-throughput mutagenesis of key candidate genes. We will first optimize these techniques by targeting the visible marker gene cinnabar, then apply the most efficient method to disrupt specific OBPs (e.g., OBP12b') and desaturase enzyme genes potentially involved in CHC production or detection. The resulting phenotypic changes in worker behavior and colony social organization will be assessed. This functional genetic approach will directly test the role of specific supergene components in orchestrating complex social traits.

Keywords: social chromosome “supergene”, odorant-binding proteins, cuticular hydrocarbon.

items.name: Mu-En Chen
items.title: Identifying the complementary sex determination gene in Solenopsis invicta

abstract.authors: Mu-En Chen*, Yu-Ching Huang , Tiffany C. Chang, John Wang
abstract.abstract: In most ant colonies, workers are sterile, yet their labor is essential for colony survival. Since all workers are diploid females while males are typically haploid and do not perform worker tasks, proper sex determination is crucial for colony function. We have confirmed that the fire ant, Solenopsis invicta, uses complementary sex determination (CSD). QTL mapping indicates that the primary sex determination locus likely contains a novel non-coding gene rather than the homologs of known hymenopteran primary sex determination genes. The fire ant candidate primary sex determination gene maps to a 15kb region, which corresponds to a hypervariable region within a conserved syntenic genomic position across hymenopteran lineages. We annotated the region and also generated RNA-seq which revealed a long non-coding RNA, HVRt. We also used ATAC-seq to examine the chromatin accessibility pattern within this region. RT-PCR experiments also suggest the expression of HVRt is detectable at the earliest stage of embryonic development, consistent with the expected timing of a primary sex determining signal. Currently, we are conducting CRISPR/Cas9 mutagenesis and RNA interference experiments to test if HVRt is the primary sex determination gene in the fire ant.

items.name: Hiroki Matsumura
items.title: Colony composition and queen polymorphism of Myrmecina amamiana (Hymenoptera: Formicidae)

abstract.authors: Hiroki Matsumura*, Hiroki Kawaoka, Shogo Makita, Hayato Shinohara, Takumi Ogino, Soichiro Somada, Saki Tada, Hajime Sasaki, Satoshi Miyazaki, Adam Khalife, Riou Mizuno, Fuminori Ito
abstract.abstract: Dispersal of social insects involves independent colony foundation (ICF) and dependent colony foundation (DCF). ICF enables long-distance dispersal but has low founding success, whereas DCF has the opposite trade-off. The ant genus Myrmecina is notable for its diversity of queen morphology and dispersal strategies. We discovered that Myrmecina amamiana has three distinct queen morphs: large and small alate queens (LAQ and SAQ, both winged) and ergatoid queens (EQ, permanently wingless). Field surveys, dissections, and morphometric analysis revealed distinct social characteristics related to queen morphs. The numbers of ovarioles in LAQ, SAQ, EQ, and workers are 4.3 ± 0.6, 4.2 ± 0.4, 6.1 ± 0.3, and 2.2 ± 0.6, respectively. Colonies were small (12.4 ± 9.1 workers) and nested preferentially in shallow (<10 cm), compact clay outcrops. AQ-monogynous, EQ-monogynous, EQ-polygynous, and queenless colonies were found, but no AQ-polygynous or AQ-EQ mixed colonies occurred. AQ and EQ were produced exclusively in AQ and EQ colonies, respectively. SAQ tends to be produced in smaller AQ colonies while LAQ is produced in larger AQ colonies. To our knowledge, this is the first known case of three distinct queen morphs in ants, suggesting remarkable reproductive polymorphism.

items.name: Hayato Shinohara
items.aff: The United Graduate School of Agricultural Sciences, Ehime University
items.title: Host dependence and the nature of the interspecific association between the cleptobiotic ant Strumigenys incerta and its host Cryptopone sauteri

abstract.authors: Hayato Shinohara*, Ryota Hosokawa, Shogo Makita, Hiroki Matsumura, Takumi Ogino, Hajime Sasaki, Toshiharu Akino, Fuminori Ito
abstract.abstract: Cleptobiosis in ants is a form of compound nesting in which one species steals food from another, yet host dependence and host impacts remain poorly understood. We investigated the cleptobiotic association between the attine ant Strumigenys incerta and its ponerine host Cryptopone sauteri. Field surveys showed that S. incerta nested exclusively within C. sauteri nests, and laboratory rearing showed substantial colony growth only in the presence of the host. Behavioral assays revealed that S. incerta primarily stole prey temporarily stored by host workers and rarely hunted independently. After host removal, workers attempted to hunt, but their success was significantly lower than that of congeneric species, indicating strong dependence on cleptobiosis for food acquisition. Host aggression toward S. incerta was rare, and S. incerta typically remained motionless with retracted appendages during encounters. Cuticular hydrocarbon analyses showed distinct profiles between the species, providing no evidence for chemical mimicry. The presence of S. incerta had no detectable effect on host colony growth. These findings indicate that S. incerta is an obligate cleptobiont and that its association with C. sauteri is close to commensalism.

items.name: Hiroyuki Shimoji
items.title: How do ants manage fecal waste within the nest?

abstract.authors: Yasunari Tanaka, Akari Nishina, Issa Kajimoto, Toshiharu Akino, Hiroyuki Shimoji*
abstract.abstract: Many ant species live at high densities in enclosed nests, where the introduction of pathogenic microorganisms can potentially lead to disease transmission among colony members. To reduce such risks, ants have evolved diverse forms of social hygiene behavior, collectively referred to as social immunity. Here, we focused on fecal waste, a potential carrier of pathogenic microorganisms and investigated how ants manage feces within the nest. First, using the ponerine ant Diacamma cf. indicum, which is known to deposit feces collectively in designated toilet areas, we examined the mechanisms underlying toilet formation through behavioral experiments. We then conducted simulations incorporating fecal odor and nest spatial structure. Our results suggest that, in D. cf. indicum, fecal odor promotes fecal aggregation, whereas toilet location is strongly influenced by spatial features of the nest. Finally, we examined toilet formation across 40 ant species and found that clearly defined toilet areas were formed in almost all species tested. Together, these results suggest that spatially organized fecal management is widespread among ants and may represent an important component of social hygiene within the nest.

items.name: Osuke Iwaki
items.title: Lethal male-male fights in the Schizotetranychus brevisetosus Ehara

abstract.authors: *Osuke Iwaki  Katsura Ito
abstract.abstract: In many animals, individuals engage in contests over resources such as food and mating opportunities. However, lethal fights are rare because the conditions favoring their evolution are limited. The spider mite is a group that includes several species showing lethal male-male fights. Because these species maintain many unmated females within their silk nests, winner males monopolize females capable of mating. At present, however, few studies have reported proximate factors that cause such fights. We established four experimental treatments: a nest containing an egg, a nest containing a female, a nest without an occupant, and no nest, and compared the proportions of lethal male–male fights among the treatments. In this study, we investigated whether the frequency of lethal fights in Schizotetranychus brevisetosus Ehara depends on the female age or the presence of the nest itself, and demonstrated that lethal fights were affected only by the nest presence. These results suggest that males fight to defend the nest, which provides future mating opportunities.

items.name: Satoshi Kusunose
items.title: Laboratory observations of phoresy in a Japanese chernetid pseudoscorpion

abstract.authors: Satoshi Kusunose*  Katsura Ito
abstract.abstract:
Phoresy is a dispersal strategy in which animals use another species for transportation. Phoresy occurs in various taxa, but is most common among small arthropods. However, the behavior of phoretic animals from attachment to detachment has not been well described.
Pseudoscorpions form phoretic associations with a wide range of hosts, such as Coleoptera, Diptera, and Hymenoptera. In this study, we report phoretic behavior in a Haplochernes sp. (Chernetidae) under laboratory conditions. 
When pseudoscorpions and longhorn beetles (Chlorophorus japonicus or Monochamus subfasciatus shikokuensis) were placed together in a Petri dish, pseudoscorpions attached to the beetles’ antennae or legs. These individuals were also observed repeatedly swaying their bodies while grasping the beetles with their pedipalps. Furthermore, they moved along the beetles’ antennae using their pedipalps.
This behavior may be involved in maintaining phoresy by selecting a position on the host.

items.name: Tzi-Yuan Wang
items.title: Luminescent characteristics and COI barcodes in 21 Taiwanese fireflies and one introduced Pygoluciola species

abstract.authors: Tzi-Yuan Wang1*, Ming-Luen Jeng2, Chih-Chieh Hsieh3, Ming-Te Chiu4, Liang-Jong Wang5
abstract.abstract: This study used a portable spectrometer to characterize peak emission wavelength (λmax) and luminescent intensity of 20 native and one introduced firefly species in Taiwan, combined with cytochrome oxidase I (COI) barcoding to clarify phylogenetic relationships. Average λmax ranged from 551 nm (green-yellow) to 579 nm (yellow-orange), with Lampyrinae showing narrower ranges than the more diverse Luciolinae. Mean luminescent intensity ranged from 0.1–3.2 lux, with Abscondita cerata and Pyrocoelia analis among the brightest species. Ambient light measurements confirmed that fireflies began flashing at 2–10 nW/cm² and took flight below 0.2–1.5 nW/cm², supporting flash intensity as a nocturnal activity cue. Phylogenetic analysis revealed substantial taxonomic ambiguity, including paraphyly within Abscondita, Luciola, Aquatica, and Curtos, and between Diaphanes and Pyrocoelia. Several public Chinese COI sequences were identified as likely misidentifications, while new sequences from China and Southeast Asia resolved monophyly in Abscondita. Additional cryptic lineages were detected within Luciola, Aquatica, and Curtos, suggesting underestimated regional diversity. These results show that integrating portable luminescent measurements with COI barcoding provides a robust framework for firefly taxonomy and habitat characterization, offering practical parameters for firefly-friendly habitat design and emphasizing careful species verification before public database submission.

items.name: Takefumi Nakazawa
items.title: Surname match/mismatch revisited: it may no longer matter for partner choice

abstract.authors: Takefumi Nakazawa*, Shinohara Naoto, Fukano Yuya
abstract.abstract: Kin recognition plays a crucial role in mating across diverse taxa by helping prevent inbreeding. In humans, surnames have historically served as indicators of kinship, and same-surname marriages were prohibited or discouraged in some societies. Here, we tested whether surnames still influence partner choice in modern society using nationwide name databases from Taiwan. In 2018, same-surname marriages occurred less frequently than expected, consistent with historical taboos against such marriages. However, this pattern was absent in 2023, suggesting a recent shift in social attitudes. To further explore this trend, we conducted a questionnaire survey among university students. Attractiveness ratings of opposite-sex face images were not significantly affected by whether the surname matched that of the respondent, contrasting with traditional customs. Although preliminary, these results suggest that the role of surname match or mismatch in partner choice may be diminishing under rapidly changing socio-cultural conditions. Further studies across regions and generations are needed to clarify how modernization and globalization reshape the role of surnames in human mate choice.

items.name: Riku Handa
items.aff: Faculty of Agriculture and Marine Science, Kochi University
items.title: Understanding the biogeography of the Shikoku-endemic trechine beetle genus Ryugadous based on comparative morphology and molecular phylogeny

abstract.authors: *Riku Handa, Keigo Uematsu
abstract.abstract:
Cave-dwelling organisms exhibit extremely low dispersal ability due to specialized adaptations to subterranean environments, including the reduction of eyes and wings, making them suitable models for studies of speciation and biogeographic history. Among them, cave trechine beetles (Carabidae:Trechini) frequently form distinct lineages restricted to individual cave systems.
Shikoku Island is a hotspot of trechine diversity in Japan, harboring 17 of the 32 genera known from Japan, including eight endemic genera. One of these, the genus Ryugadous, has been divided into the subgenera Ryugadous and Yuadorgus based on morphological characteristics, but their phylogenetic relationships have not been tested using molecular data.
In this study, we investigated the relationships between the two subgenera using comparative morphology and molecular phylogenetic analyses. Maximum likelihood and Bayesian analyses of nuclear and mitochondrial DNA sequences recovered Ryugadous as a monophyletic lineage, with Yuadorgus positioned outside this clade. Morphological comparisons revealed that species of Ryugadous possess large and complex copulatory pieces with well-developed teeth patches, whereas Yuadorgus exhibits simpler genital structures. Our results are consistent with the previous taxonomy and provide a basis for future studies of the evolution and biogeography of subterranean beetles in Shikoku.

items.name: Mia Prastika Devi
items.title: Biodiversity of Caenorhabditis Nematodes in Southeast Asia and Taiwan

abstract.authors: Mia Prastika Devi*, Fibrianti Shinta Dewi, Hagus Tarno, Viet Dai Dang, John Wang
abstract.abstract: Species delimitation in Caenorhabditis nematodes is commonly based on an initial assessment using sequence identity at the ITS2 barcode and confirmed by mating tests for compatibility. To date, when two independent isolates, or strains, have ITS2 sequence identity <96.0%, they have always been different species. In contrast, strains with >99.0% identity have reliably indicated reproductively compatible. We have been using this framework to study the biodiversity of Caenorhabditis in Taiwan and Southeast Asia, and here we report our recent surveys results. Interestingly, for three strains ITS2 sequence identity was >96% to its nearest species, but the closest pairs were reproductively incompatible in all cases. Because ITS2 is only one nuclear sequence, we sequenced, assembled, and annotated the mitochondrial genomes for these three strains. Mitogenomic phylogenetic analysis matched the ITS2 analysis for two strains but not a third, indicating that these two markers can conflict. Overall, we have identified three new cryptic species. Our results raise the possibility that other cryptic Caenorhabditis species have already been isolated but assigned incorrectly to known species based on high ITS2 sequence identity.

items.name: Shunsuke Mori
items.aff: Ushimado Marine Institute, Faculty of Science, Okayama University
items.title: Functional Divergence of GnRH/Corazonin Signaling Revealed by Early-Diverging Bilaterians, Acoel and Polyclad Flatworms

abstract.authors: Shunsuke Mori*, Akira Shiraishi, Toshio Sekiguchi, Ryo Nakamura, Tatsuya Sakamoto, Hirotaka Sakamoto, Honoo Satake, Mayuko Hamada
abstract.abstract: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) signaling regulates diverse physiological processes across bilaterians. It primarily regulates sexual maturation in deuterostomes and energy metabolism in protostomes, but its ancestral function and how it diversified during evolution remain unclear. To clarify the evolutionary origin of GnRH signaling, we investigated two early-diverging bilaterian models: the acoel Praesagittifera naikaiensis and the polyclad flatworm Comoplana pusilla. Phylogenetic analysis revealed that acoel GnRH receptors cluster with vertebrate GnRHRs, whereas polyclad flatworm receptors group with arthropod corazonin receptors. In both animals, GnRH family peptides are synthesized in neurons of the central nervous system. Moreover, low-temperature treatment increased GnRH transcript levels in both species. Despite this shared temperature responsiveness, downstream functional responses differed between the two species: in acoels, GnRH peptide administration increased expression of the germline marker (nanos) and promoted reproductive organ development. In contrast, GnRH treatment in polyclad flatworms suppressed the expression of energy metabolism-related gene without affecting nanos expression. These results indicate that low-temperature responsiveness is a conserved feature of ancestral GnRH signaling, whereas its downstream physiological functions have diversified among bilaterian lineages. Our findings suggest that the functional divergence of GnRH signaling into deuterostome-type (sexual maturation) and protostome-type (metabolic regulation) may have occurred around the protostome-deuterostome split.

oral.format: Please prepare your slides in 16:9 widescreen format. For compatibility, we recommend using the default settings in Windows 11 and PowerPoint 2024. Accepted file formats are .pptx and .pdf.
oral.timing: Each 15-minute contributed oral slot includes 12 minutes for the talk, 2 minutes for questions and 1 minute for speaker changeover. Bell reminders:
bells: Two minutes of speaking time remain.
Please finish your talk and begin the Q&A.
Please conclude the Q&A and allow 1 minute for the next speaker.
oral.symposium: Symposium speakers: please reserve 1 minute for speaker changeover within each allocated slot. Talk and Q&A lengths vary by symposium; please follow your session chair. All scheduled start and end times remain unchanged.
oral.slot: Each 15-minute contributed oral slot includes 12 minutes for the talk, 2 minutes for questions and 1 minute for speaker changeover.

poster.intro: Please display your poster on the board bearing your assigned poster number.
poster.size: Please prepare and print an A0 portrait poster: 84.1 cm wide × 118.9 cm high. The boards are in portrait orientation; smaller posters are also welcome.
poster.supplies: Poster mounting supplies will be provided on site.
poster.care: Please take care of your poster and remove it by the deadline. The organizers and venue cannot be responsible for its safekeeping. Posters left after the removal deadline may be taken down or discarded by the organizers.
